course.title: Materials and Manufacturing
course.description: What materials are made of, how they fail, how things are shaped, and how to choose a material and process together.
course.audience: Adults who know stress and strain and basic chemistry and want to understand why parts are made of what they are and how.

paragraphs: A tensile test pulls a bar until it breaks and records only the force and the stretch, yet from that record you can read the handful of numbers that decide whether a material suits a bridge, a spring or a window. Materials science asks why a material has the numbers it does, and the answers lie far below anything you can see, in the bonds between its atoms, the defects in its crystals and, for steel, a fraction of a percent of carbon whose arrangement depends on how fast the metal was cooled.

Manufacturing is the other half of the subject, since a material is only useful once it has been given a shape, and each way of shaping it has limits that can be worked out before any metal is poured or cut. A casting freezes at a rate set by its volume and its surface, a forging needs a force set by the metal's flow stress and the area it is pressed over, and a cutting tool wears out at a rate that rises steeply with its speed, so most of the practical questions in a workshop come down to a short formula and a number.

The two halves meet in every real part, because the material that suits a job best on paper still has to be made into the right shape, in the right quantity and at a sensible cost. With both in hand you can rank materials for a particular job, work out when an expensive mould pays for itself, and check whether a process can hold the tolerance on a drawing, all with short calculations.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a stress-strain curve and name the properties it shows.
You'll be able to use the lever rule on steel and explain heat treatment.
You'll be able to compute the stress at which a crack grows and the metal lost to corrosion.
You'll be able to compute casting, forming and machining quantities.
You'll be able to choose a material with a performance index.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Engineering: Structures and Machines, Chemistry: Atoms to Reactions, Probability and Statistics.

modules.title: What materials are and do
modules.description: The measurements that describe a material, and the structure that explains them.

modules.title: Steels, polymers, ceramics, composites
modules.description: How phase, chain and fibre structure give each family its character, and how each fails.

modules.title: Shaping and making
modules.description: Casting, forming, machining, moulding and additive: what each does to the material and the cost.

modules.title: Quality and choice
modules.description: Holding tolerance in production and choosing a material and process together.

concepts.title: Yield and ultimate strength
concepts.summary: Yield is where permanent deformation starts; ultimate strength is the highest engineering stress before necking.

concepts.title: Ductility
concepts.summary: How far a material stretches before it breaks, reported as percent elongation or reduction in area.

concepts.title: Toughness
concepts.summary: The energy absorbed per volume up to fracture, the area under the stress-strain curve.

concepts.title: Bonding
concepts.summary: Metallic, ionic, covalent and van der Waals bonds set stiffness, melting point and brittleness.

concepts.title: Specific stiffness
concepts.summary: Young's modulus divided by density, a measure of stiffness for a given mass.

concepts.title: Dislocation
concepts.summary: A line defect whose motion lets metal layers slip one atom row at a time, so metals yield far below ideal strength.

concepts.title: Hall-Petch relation
concepts.summary: Yield strength rises as grain size falls: s = s0 + k/sqrt(d).

concepts.title: Eutectoid steel
concepts.summary: Steel with about 0.76 percent carbon turns wholly to pearlite when cooled slowly through 727 C.

concepts.title: Martensite
concepts.summary: Fast quenching traps carbon in a strained, very hard structure; tempering trades some hardness for toughness.

concepts.title: Glass transition
concepts.summary: Below Tg a polymer is hard and glassy; above it, soft and rubbery.

concepts.title: Rule of mixtures
concepts.summary: Along the fibres, Ec = Vf Ef + (1-Vf) Em; across, 1/Ec = Vf/Ef + (1-Vf)/Em.

concepts.title: Fracture toughness
concepts.summary: K_IC is the stress intensity at which a crack grows; K = Y s sqrt(pi a).

concepts.title: Ductile-brittle transition
concepts.summary: Many steels turn brittle below a transition temperature, so a crack runs without yielding first.

concepts.title: Galvanic corrosion
concepts.summary: When two metals touch in an electrolyte, the more reactive one corrodes.

concepts.title: Faraday's law
concepts.summary: Mass lost m = I t M/(n F), with F = 96485 C/mol.

concepts.title: Chvorinov's rule
concepts.summary: Solidification time t = B (V/A)^2, with V volume and A cooling surface area.

concepts.title: Shrinkage
concepts.summary: Metal contracts when it solidifies and cools, so patterns are made oversize.

concepts.title: True strain
concepts.summary: e = ln(h0/h1) for a thickness reduction; true strains add.

concepts.title: Hot and cold working
concepts.summary: Working above roughly 0.4 of the melting temperature in kelvin recrystallises the grains as they form.

concepts.title: Material removal rate
concepts.summary: In turning, MRR = v f d, the product of cutting speed, feed and depth of cut.

concepts.title: Taylor tool life
concepts.summary: V T^n = C: raising cutting speed shortens tool life sharply.

concepts.title: Clamp force
concepts.summary: Mould halves are held shut against cavity pressure x projected area.

concepts.title: Break-even volume
concepts.summary: Tooling cost divided by the saving per part.

concepts.title: Process capability
concepts.summary: Cp = (USL - LSL)/(6 sigma): how much room the spec has against process spread.

concepts.title: Cpk
concepts.summary: Cpk = min(USL - mean, mean - LSL)/(3 sigma): capability with centring included.

concepts.title: Performance index
concepts.summary: A combination of properties that one number ranks; for a light stiff beam, maximise sqrt(E)/density.

concepts.title: Process fit
concepts.summary: A process suits a combination of shape, size, material, volume and tolerance.

lessons.title: What a tensile test tells you

steps.headline: A tensile test turns force and stretch into stress and strain, and the first part of the curve is a straight line whose slope is the stiffness.

lead.text: The machine records the force F on the bar and the distance between the two gauge marks. Dividing the force by the bar's original cross-sectional area A0 gives the **engineering stress**, which is F / A0, and dividing the increase in gauge length by the original gauge length L0 gives the **engineering strain**, which is the extension divided by L0. Using the original dimensions throughout is what makes the curve a property of the material, because a thick bar and a thin bar of the same steel then trace the same line.

For a small pull the line is straight, so stress is proportional to strain, and its slope is the **Young's modulus** E, about 210 GPa for steel. This holds while the deformation is **elastic**, meaning that the bar returns to its original length when the load is removed. The figure starts with that stretch, drawn larger than it really is, since for steel it spans only about 0.1 percent of strain.

afterFigure.text: The slope E says how much a bar stretches under a given stress. It says nothing about how large a stress the bar can take, which is what *strength* means. An aluminium alloy has an E of about 70 GPa, so it stretches three times as far as steel under the same stress, and yet some aluminium alloys are as strong as some steels. The figure steps through the points on the curve that the rest of this lesson names.

diagram.alt: A stress-strain curve for low-carbon steel with four stages: a steep straight elastic line, the yield point near 250 MPa, the peak at the ultimate tensile strength near 400 MPa, and fracture after the curve has fallen.
diagram.caption: Engineering stress against engineering strain. Use the buttons to move through the four stages of the curve.

reveal.text: The bar stretches by about half a millimetre in each metre of length, which is why steel looks rigid under ordinary loads.
Beyond yield, part of the stretch is permanent. The next screen shows where that begins, and how it is found when the curve has no obvious corner.

steps.headline: Yield strength is the stress at which permanent deformation begins, and a curve with no sharp corner is read with a 0.2 percent offset line.

lead.text: At some stress the straight line ends and strain begins to grow faster than stress. From there on, unloading follows a new line *parallel* to the elastic one, so the bar comes back only part of the way and keeps a permanent stretch called **plastic deformation**. The stress at which this begins is the **yield strength**. Annealed low-carbon steel has a sharp yield point near 250 MPa, but aluminium alloys and many others bend away from the elastic line gradually, and there is no corner to point at.

afterFigure.text: For those the convention is the **0.2 percent offset method**. Draw a line with the elastic slope E that starts at 0.002 on the strain axis, and the stress where it crosses the curve is taken as the yield strength. It is the stress that, once removed, leaves a permanent strain of 0.2 percent, a small but measurable amount that engineers have agreed to treat as the practical start of yielding. The figure shows the construction, and then the permanent strain left by unloading from beyond yield.

diagram.alt: A gradual stress-strain curve for an aluminium alloy with no sharp yield point. A line with the elastic slope starts at 0.002 on the strain axis and crosses the curve at the yield strength. A second view shows unloading from beyond yield along a line parallel to the elastic one, leaving permanent strain.
diagram.caption: Two views of an aluminium-like curve: the 0.2 percent offset construction, and the permanent strain left after unloading from beyond yield.

reveal.text: Where this line meets the curve is the yield strength. The offset line shifts the elastic line sideways by a fixed 0.2 percent of strain at every stress.

steps.headline: The ultimate tensile strength is the peak of the engineering stress curve, and the fall after it comes from the shrinking area of the neck.

lead.text: Past yield the metal gets stronger as it is stretched, a behaviour called **strain hardening**, so a larger stress is needed for each further step in strain. The highest engineering stress the bar reaches is its **ultimate tensile strength**, about 400 MPa for annealed low-carbon steel. Around that point the stretching stops being uniform and concentrates in one short section of the bar that narrows into a **neck**, as the opening figure showed.

afterFigure.text: After the peak the curve falls, and it is tempting to read this as the metal weakening. The metal in the neck is still hardening. What falls is the *engineering* stress, because it divides the force by the original area A0, whereas the neck's area is now much smaller. The **true stress**, the force divided by the area the bar actually has at that moment, keeps rising until the bar fractures, and the figure shows both curves.

diagram.alt: Two views of the steel curve beyond the peak. The first shows the engineering stress curve rising to a peak and then falling. The second adds the true stress curve, which keeps rising until fracture.
diagram.caption: Engineering stress divides by the original area. True stress divides by the area at that moment.

cases.label: Engineering stress
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><defs><marker id="t1-h" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><line class="s-ink w2" x1="90" y1="300" x2="90" y2="40" marker-end="url(#t1-h)"/><line class="s-ink w2" x1="90" y1="300" x2="600" y2="300" marker-end="url(#t1-h)"/><text class="t-small t-muted" x="98" y="38" text-anchor="start">stress</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="600" y="320" text-anchor="end">strain</text><polyline class="f-none s-accent w3" points="90,300 125,175 134,174.4 143,173.8 152,173.2 161,172.6 170,172.0 181.5,166.7 193.0,161.5 204.5,156.4 216.0,151.3 227.5,146.4 239.0,141.6 250.5,137.0 262.0,132.6 273.5,128.5 285.0,124.6 296.5,121.1 308.0,117.8 319.5,114.9 331.0,112.3 342.5,110.1 354.0,108.3 365.5,106.9 377.0,105.8 388.5,105.2 400.0,105.0 408.0,105.5 416.0,106.8 424.0,109.0 432.0,112.2 440.0,116.2 448.0,121.2 456.0,127.0 464.0,133.8 472.0,141.4 480.0,150.0"/><circle class="f-accent s-accent w2" cx="400" cy="105" r="6"/><text class="t-small t-accent" x="400" y="84" text-anchor="middle">peak</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="98" y="348" text-anchor="start">Engineering stress divides the force by the original area A0 all the way.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The engineering curve is a convenient record because the original area is known before the test, even though the real area in the neck is changing.

steps.headline: Ductility is measured by how far a bar stretches or narrows before it breaks, as percent elongation and percent reduction in area.

lead.text: Fit the two halves of the broken bar together and measure the distance between the gauge marks. The **percent elongation** is the increase in gauge length divided by the original gauge length, multiplied by 100. The neck is measured as well, because the **reduction in area** compares the original area A0 with the area Af at the fracture surface, as 100 x (A0 - Af) / A0. Both numbers tell you how much plastic deformation a material can take, and a material with a high value is called **ductile**, while one that breaks with almost none is **brittle**.

afterFigure.text: A ductile metal gives warning, because it deforms visibly before it breaks, and that is one reason structures are usually built from ductile steels. Glass gives none. The figure shows the measurements taken from a 10 mm bar with a 50 mm gauge length, which the next two screens use.

diagram.alt: A bar before and after a tensile test. Before, the gauge length is 50 mm and the diameter is 10 mm. After fracture, the gauge length is 60 mm and the diameter at the neck is 8 mm.

workedSteps.text: The original area follows from the 10 mm diameter, using area = pi x d squared / 4.
The area at the fracture surface uses the 8 mm diameter in the same way.

steps.headline: Toughness is the area under the stress-strain curve, which makes it a different property from strength, stiffness and hardness.

lead.text: A stress multiplied by a strain is an energy per unit volume, because a stress in MPa is the same as MJ per cubic metre and a strain has no units. The area under the whole curve is therefore the energy that every cubic metre of the material absorbs before it fractures, and this is the **toughness**. Glass has a steep elastic line and breaks at a very small strain with no plastic region, so its area is tiny. A low-carbon steel stretches a long way at a high stress, so its area is large. Rubber carries little stress, but it stretches several times its length, so it absorbs a good deal of energy too.

afterFigure.text: Four words that are often used as if they meant the same thing measure different quantities. **Stiffness** is the slope in the elastic region, **strength** is the stress at yield or at the peak, toughness is the area, and **hardness** is resistance to indentation, which is found in a separate test. A material can have any of the four without the others: glass is stiff and hard, but it is not tough.

diagram.alt: Stress-strain curves for steel, glass and rubber, with the area under each curve shaded. Steel has a large area, glass a tiny one because it breaks at a very small strain, and rubber an area from low stress over a large strain.

lessons.reviewLabel: What a tensile test tells you
lessons.nextAction: Link the properties you can measure in a tensile test to the bonds between atoms and the four families of material.

blocks.text: A steel bar 10 mm across, clamped in a testing machine and pulled until it breaks, will stretch by around a fifth of its length before it does so, while a bar of window glass of the same size snaps with no visible stretch at all. The machine records only two things as it pulls, the force on the bar and the distance between two marks drawn on it, yet from those two records a handful of numbers can be read that decide whether a material suits a bridge girder, a spring or a window.

Both records depend on the size of the bar as well as on the material, so they are divided by the bar's original area and by the original 50 mm between the marks, which turns them into a curve of stress against strain that any bar of the same steel would trace. From that curve you can read how stiff the material is, the stress at which it starts to stretch for good and the highest stress it can carry, how far it stretches before it breaks and how much energy it absorbs, and these are the numbers the rest of the course uses to compare one material with another.

intro.whyItMatters: These numbers are the vocabulary the rest of the course uses to compare materials.

recap.keyIdea: A tensile test gives a curve whose slope is stiffness, whose yield and peak are strength, whose end-point strain and neck are ductility, and whose area is toughness.

blocks.text: Loading a bar produces a curve of engineering stress against strain: the straight part has slope E, permanent deformation starts at the yield strength, and the highest point is the ultimate tensile strength, after which the neck makes the engineering stress fall. Ductility is read from the broken bar as percent elongation, the extension divided by the original gauge length, and as reduction in area, and toughness is the area under the whole curve.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks why materials have the stiffness and density they do, starting from the bonds between atoms.

lessons.title: Bonds, density and the four families

steps.headline: The stiffness of a material comes from how steeply the force between two atoms rises as they are pulled apart, and the kind of bond sets that slope.

lead.text: Atoms sit at the spacing where the forces between them balance, and pulling them apart brings an attraction back that grows with the separation. Near that spacing the force is close to proportional to the stretch, so each bond behaves like a small spring, and the slope of the curve in the opening figure is the spring's stiffness. Add up billions of these springs in parallel and in series and you get the stretch of a whole bar, which is why a material's Young's modulus is set by the bonds inside it.

Bonds fall into four kinds. In a **metallic bond** the outer electrons belong to the whole piece, and the positive ions sit in that shared sea. In an **ionic bond** a positive and a negative ion attract each other, and in a **covalent bond** a pair of atoms shares electrons. These three are strong. The fourth, the **secondary bond**, is a weak attraction between molecules or chains, and the figure shows each in turn.

afterFigure.text: Strong bonds give a steep slope and so a high E, while secondary bonds give a shallow one. The figure also shows why the bond type matters to more than stiffness: whether atoms can slide past one another depends on how directional their bonds are, and that decides if a material is ductile or brittle.

diagram.alt: Four drawings of atomic bonding. Metallic bonding shows positive ions in a sea of electrons, ionic bonding shows alternating positive and negative ions, covalent bonding shows pairs of atoms sharing electrons, and secondary bonding shows chains held together by weak dashed attractions.
diagram.caption: The four kinds of bond. Use the buttons to compare them.

lead.text: A polyethylene molecule is a long chain of carbon atoms, each joined to the next by a strong bond, but the bond that holds one chain to its neighbour is of a different kind.

reveal.text: Warming the polymer lets the chains slide past each other, because only the weak bonds between them have to be overcome.
Strong bonds make the elastic line steep, but they do nothing for the plastic region, which needs atoms that can slide.

steps.headline: Engineering materials fall into four families, and each family's usual bonding explains its usual properties.

lead.text: Metals are held by metallic bonds, which let layers slide, so they are stiff, strong and ductile, and they conduct heat and electricity. Ceramics and glasses are held by ionic and covalent bonds that resist both stretching and sliding, so they are very stiff, hard and strong in compression, and they are brittle in tension. Polymers are long covalent chains held together by secondary bonds, which gives them low stiffness and low density and lets them soften when warmed. Composites combine two materials, most often strong fibres in a polymer, to get properties that neither has alone.

afterFigure.text: Notice that strong bonds do not make a material tough. A ceramic has bonds as strong as any, and yet it breaks with almost no warning, because nothing in it can deform to absorb energy, as the toughness area of the last lesson showed. Toughness needs the bonds to let planes of atoms slide, which a metallic bond does and a covalent or ionic bond does not.

steps.headline: Dividing a material's stiffness by its density gives its stiffness per unit mass, and on that measure the common metals are almost equal.

lead.text: A designer who wants a light part needs stiffness for each kilogram, so the useful number is E divided by density, known as the **specific stiffness**. With E in GPa and density in g/cm3, steel has an E of 210 against aluminium's 70, three times as much, while its density of 7.85 is also close to three times aluminium's 2.70. Dividing one by the other therefore cancels the two effects almost exactly, so the two metals come out within a few percent of each other.

afterFigure.text: The charts make this visible. The first two show E and density separately, where steel towers over aluminium, and the third shows the ratio, where the metals sit side by side and nylon, at about a tenth of them, stands apart. Only a change of family changes the ratio by a large factor.

diagram.alt: Three bar charts for steel, titanium, aluminium, a glass-fibre composite and nylon: stiffness E in GPa, density in g/cm3, and stiffness divided by density. The first three metals and the composite come out similar, and nylon is about a tenth of them.
diagram.caption: Steel is three times as stiff as aluminium and about three times as dense, so per unit density they come out almost equal. Use the buttons to move between the charts.

steps.headline: Find the specific stiffness of steel, with E = 210 GPa and density 7.85 g/cm3.

workedSteps.text: Specific stiffness compares the stiffness E with a second property, so that materials can be compared for each kilogram.
Put in the values for steel, keeping E in GPa and the density in g/cm3.
Dividing gives a little under 27, which is 26.8 to one decimal place.

steps.headline: Find the specific stiffness of titanium, with E = 116 GPa and density 4.5 g/cm3.

workedSteps.text: The method is the same as for steel, so the quantity to work out is E divided by the density.
Substituting the values for titanium gives 116 / 4.5. Work it out to one decimal place.

reveal.text: Its specific stiffness is only about a tenth of the metals', which follows from the secondary bonds between its chains.

steps.headline: A polymer is soft because of its weak secondary bonds, and reinforcing it with fibres removes most of that weakness.

lead.text: It is easy to conclude that plastics are weak by nature, and that metals are the only way to stiffness. The nylon bar in the charts supports the first half of this, since a bulk polymer's stiffness is limited by the secondary bonds between its chains. A fibre is different: glass or carbon fibres are covalent along their whole length, so they are stiff, and when they are embedded in a polymer the composite takes most of its stiffness from them. A glass-fibre composite with E = 40 GPa and a density of 1.9 g/cm3 comes far closer to the metals on this measure than nylon does, and carbon fibre does better still.

afterFigure.text: This is also why aluminium is not preferred over steel for its stiffness per unit mass. The two are almost equal on that measure, and the reasons to choose one over the other lie elsewhere, which the last lessons of this course take up.

reveal.text: It reaches roughly 80 percent of steel's value at one quarter of its density, and that is how a plastic ends up competing with metals.

lessons.orientation: Link bonding to the properties of metals, ceramics and polymers and compare materials by specific stiffness.
lessons.reviewLabel: Bonds, density and the four families
lessons.nextAction: Look inside a metal and see how its crystals and dislocations make it weaker than its bonds suggest.

blocks.text: Pull on a steel wire with a stress of 200 MPa and it stretches by about 0.1 percent, while a nylon cord of the same size under the same stress stretches by almost 7 percent, around seventy times as much. The shape is the same in both cases, so the difference lies in the material, and more exactly in what holds its atoms together.

Each pair of neighbouring atoms is held at a resting spacing by a bond, and pulling them slightly further apart is resisted by a force that grows in step with the stretch, so for small loads a bond behaves like a spring. How stiff that spring is depends on the kind of bond, and since a material's stiffness is the combined stiffness of billions of such springs, the kind of bond is what explains why engineering materials fall into four families with such different properties.

diagram.alt: Two curves of the force between a pair of atoms against their separation. Both cross zero at the resting spacing r0. The curve for a strong bond is steep at r0, and the curve for a weak bond is shallow.
diagram.caption: The slope at the resting spacing is the stiffness of the bond. A steep slope means a large force for a small stretch.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the four kinds of bond, match each family of material to its typical properties, and compute and compare specific stiffness.
intro.whyItMatters: It shows why a light part can be stiff or weak depending on what it is made of, before any design is attempted.

recap.keyIdea: Bonding sets stiffness and the way a material deforms, and the stiffness per unit mass, E divided by density, is almost the same for the common metals.

blocks.text: The force between atoms rises steeply for strong metallic, ionic and covalent bonds and shallowly for the secondary bonds between chains, which is why metals and ceramics are stiff and polymers are not. Strong bonds do not make a material tough, since ceramics resist sliding and break with little warning. Dividing E by density puts materials on one scale, where steel, aluminium and titanium are nearly equal at about 26 and a fibre composite reaches 21.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks why metals deform and yield at stresses far below what their bonds could carry, which needs a look at the crystal itself.

lessons.title: Why metals are weaker than their bonds

steps.headline: A metal is a crystal lattice of atoms, and an ordinary piece of metal is made of many small crystals called grains.

lead.text: The strong bonds of the last lesson hold the atoms of a metal in a regular lattice, each atom sitting at the same spacing from its neighbours. If a perfect crystal were sheared, a whole plane of atoms would have to slide over the plane beneath it, and every bond across that plane would have to stretch together. Estimates of the stress that needs come to about a tenth of the **shear modulus**, the stiffness of the metal against shearing, which for steel (G is about 80 GPa) is around 8 GPa, some thirty times the 250 MPa at which mild steel yields. The bonds are therefore not what limits a metal's strength.

Something in the real metal makes the sliding far easier, and the next screen shows what. First, it helps to know that an ordinary piece of metal is a *polycrystal*: when it solidifies, crystals start in many places and grow until they meet, so the metal is made of **grains** whose lattices point in different directions. The surfaces where grains meet are **grain boundaries**.

afterFigure.text: Each grain is a perfect-looking lattice, and each boundary is a thin region where the atoms do not line up. A typical grain is a few hundredths of a millimetre across, far smaller than anything you can see, and as the later screens show, how big the grains are changes the strength of the metal considerably.

steps.headline: Metals deform by the movement of dislocations, which carry slip across a crystal one row of atoms at a time.

lead.text: The weakness lies in a defect. Real crystals contain **dislocations**, places where an extra half plane of atoms ends inside the lattice, as the figure shows in the highlighted column. Under a shear force the half plane does not have to break the whole plane of bonds at once. The atoms next to it shift by a small distance, so that the half plane moves one atomic spacing along, then another, and the bonds that stretch at any moment are only the few along the dislocation line.

afterFigure.text: When the dislocation reaches the surface the top part of the crystal has slipped a full spacing relative to the bottom, and this repeated by many dislocations is **plastic deformation**. A ripple carried along a rug moves the rug a little at a time, and it takes far less effort than dragging the whole rug across the floor. A crystal with dislocations yields at a fraction of the ideal stress for the same reason, and a metal can only be strengthened by making their movement harder.

diagram.alt: Atoms drawn as circles in rows. An extra half plane of atoms, highlighted, ends partway down the crystal. Under a shear force it moves one atomic spacing to the right, and when it reaches the edge the top part of the crystal has slipped by one spacing, leaving a step.
diagram.caption: A dislocation moves through the crystal a little at a time, so only a few bonds are stretched at any moment. Use the buttons to follow it.

lead.text: The stress needed to keep this defect moving through the crystal is what sets a metal's [[yield strength|The stress at which permanent deformation begins. Met in the first lesson, 'What a tensile test tells you'.]].

reveal.text: Everything that strengthens a metal does so by stopping or slowing this defect, as the next screens show.
A dislocation cannot move straight across a boundary, because the slip planes on the other side point in a different direction. The next screen gives the relationship.

steps.headline: The yield strength of a metal rises as its grains get smaller, following the Hall-Petch relationship.

lead.text: A dislocation moving through a grain stops at the boundary, and the stress has to build before slip can start in the next grain. A metal with small grains has many boundaries close together, so each dislocation travels only a short distance before it is held up, and the metal is stronger. E. O. Hall in 1951 and N. J. Petch in 1953 each found that the yield strength follows a straight line when plotted against one over the square root of the grain size d, which is written strength = s0 + k / square root of d.

afterFigure.text: Here s0 is a constant stress, and k measures how strongly the boundaries resist slip. The constants for a real alloy are measured, and this lesson uses illustrative ones, s0 = 50 MPa and k = 20 MPa mm^0.5, with d in mm. Because of the square root, making grains four times smaller does not quadruple the strength: it doubles the grain term. The figure shows large and fine grains, and then the line.

diagram.alt: Two schematic grain structures and a straight-line plot. A block with a few large grains has a yield strength of 100 MPa, and a block with many small grains has 300 MPa. The plot shows yield strength rising linearly with one over the square root of grain size.
diagram.caption: Smaller grains have more boundaries to stop dislocations. The constants are illustrative, not those of a real alloy.

reveal.text: Reducing the grain size from 0.04 mm to 0.01 mm raises the strength from 150 MPa to 250 MPa. The next screen continues from this.

steps.headline: Find the yield strength of the metal with d = 0.01 mm.

workedSteps.text: The formula is strength = 50 + 20 / square root of d, and the grain size is 0.01 mm.
The square root of 0.01 is 0.1, because 0.1 times 0.1 is 0.01.
Dividing 20 by 0.1 gives the contribution of the boundaries.
Adding the constant stress gives the yield strength.

steps.headline: Find the yield strength when the grain size is reduced to d = 0.0025 mm.

workedSteps.text: The square root of 0.0025 is 0.05, because 0.05 times 0.05 is 0.0025.
The grain term is 20 divided by this square root, and the constant is added to it. Work out the yield strength.

steps.headline: Alloying and work hardening strengthen a metal in other ways, and each has a cost that smaller grains usually avoid.

lead.text: Grain size is only one way to put obstacles in the path of dislocations. In **alloying**, atoms of a different element are added: zinc atoms in copper distort the lattice around them, and a dislocation has to push through that strained region, so brass is stronger than pure copper. In **work hardening**, the metal is deformed cold, and the deformation itself multiplies the dislocations until they tangle and block each other. A copper wire drawn through dies gets harder with each pass and finally becomes brittle, because the strength that it has gained has used up some of its ability to deform.

afterFigure.text: Work hardening can be undone. **Annealing**, heating the metal so that new, strain-free grains grow in place of the deformed ones, removes the tangle of dislocations and makes the wire soft again. The cards compare the three routes. Notice that each one costs something different, so the right route depends on what else the part needs: finer grains usually keep toughness, alloying costs conductivity, and work hardening costs ductility.

diagram.alt: Three cards for the ways to strengthen a metal: smaller grains, alloying and work hardening, each with what it does and what it costs.
diagram.caption: Each route works by getting in the way of dislocations, and each has its own cost.

lead.text: The Hall-Petch relationship can also be run backwards, from the strength a design needs to the grain size that gives it.

lessons.orientation: Explain how dislocations, grain size, alloying and work hardening change strength.
lessons.reviewLabel: Why metals are weaker than their bonds
lessons.nextAction: Add carbon to iron and see how steel's strength depends on its composition and heat treatment.

blocks.text: A perfect crystal of iron would need a shearing stress of about 8 GPa before one plane of atoms slid over the next, if every bond across the plane had to stretch at once. Mild steel yields at around 250 MPa, thirty times less, and annealed pure iron yields at much less still. The bonds of the last lesson are therefore not what sets the strength of a metal, and the numbers say that something in a real crystal makes sliding far easier than the perfect case.

That something is a defect, and learning what it is explains a good deal that is otherwise odd: why a drawn wire hardens, why a bent paper clip is harder to bend a second time, and why brass is stronger than copper.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to describe how a dislocation lets a metal deform, use the Hall-Petch relationship, and choose between smaller grains, alloying and work hardening.
intro.whyItMatters: Every treatment that changes the strength of a metal does so by changing how easily dislocations move.

recap.keyIdea: A metal yields when dislocations move, so anything that obstructs them, such as grain boundaries, foreign atoms or other dislocations, makes the metal stronger.

blocks.text: Metals yield at a small fraction of the ideal strength because plastic deformation moves dislocations, which carry slip along a crystal one row at a time. Grain boundaries, alloying atoms and tangles of other dislocations all obstruct them, and the Hall-Petch relationship, strength = s0 + k / square root of d, shows the effect of grain size. Alloying costs conductivity, work hardening costs ductility and is undone by annealing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson applies these ideas to steel, where carbon content and heat treatment change the strength several times over.

lessons.title: Steel, carbon and heat treatment

steps.headline: Steel is iron with a little carbon, and which phases it forms depends on its temperature and how much carbon it holds.

lead.text: Pure iron at room temperature is a soft metal called **ferrite**. Its lattice has little room for carbon, and it can hold at most 0.022 percent by weight, so any extra carbon has to go somewhere else. It goes into **cementite**, the compound Fe3C, which holds 6.7 percent carbon and is hard and brittle. Steel is iron with between about 0.02 and 2 percent carbon, and its properties depend on how much cementite it contains and how that cementite is arranged.

Heating changes the lattice. Above about 727 C iron takes a different crystal structure called **austenite**, which can dissolve up to roughly 2 percent carbon, so a steel heated enough becomes a single uniform solid. The question that matters for heat treatment is what happens to that carbon when the steel cools back down, and the iron-carbon diagram of the next screen answers it.

afterFigure.text: A diagram that shows which phases are present at each temperature and composition is a **phase diagram**. This lesson uses a simplified version, with the temperatures and compositions of a standard materials textbook, and it keeps to steels with less than about 1.2 percent carbon.

steps.headline: When austenite cools slowly past 727 C it turns into pearlite, a layered mix of ferrite and cementite.

lead.text: The diagram has one special point: at 0.76 percent carbon and 727 C, all the austenite changes into a structure of thin alternating layers of ferrite and cementite, called **pearlite**. The change is the **eutectoid reaction**, and 0.76 percent carbon is the **eutectoid composition**. Cooling must be slow, because carbon atoms have to move through the iron to form the layers, and that movement takes time. The figure shows the diagram, and then follows two steels down it.

afterFigure.text: A steel with less carbon than 0.76 percent, a **hypoeutectoid** steel, first has to throw out ferrite, since the austenite holds more carbon than ferrite can. The 0.40 percent steel does this between the sloping line and 727 C, and the ferrite formed there is called **proeutectoid ferrite**. The austenite that remains grows richer in carbon until it reaches 0.76 percent, at 727 C, and then turns to pearlite. Just below 727 C the steel is therefore made of proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite, in proportions that the lever rule gives.

diagram.alt: A simplified iron-carbon diagram from 0 to 1.2 weight percent carbon and 600 to 950 degrees Celsius. Austenite lies above the sloping lines. Below 727 degrees steel is ferrite plus pearlite on the left of 0.76 percent carbon and pearlite plus cementite on the right. Two further views follow a 0.40 percent and a 0.76 percent carbon steel down through the diagram.
diagram.caption: A simplified iron-carbon diagram, not to scale. Use the buttons to follow a 0.40 percent carbon steel and a 0.76 percent carbon steel as they cool slowly.

reveal.text: Pearlite is part soft ferrite and part hard cementite, and its layers are fine enough to appear as a sheen under a microscope.
The extra carbon becomes extra cementite, so the more carbon there is, the more cementite the steel holds. The next screen measures that amount.

steps.headline: The lever rule gives the share of each structure from the lengths of two arms on a bar, and the share of a structure is the arm on the far side.

lead.text: Just below 727 C a steel with composition C0 is a mixture of ferrite, with 0.022 percent carbon, and pearlite, with 0.76 percent. Treat the bar from 0.022 to 0.76 as a lever with its fulcrum at C0. The fraction of pearlite is the length of the arm from ferrite to C0, divided by the length of the whole bar, so it is (C0 - 0.022) / (0.76 - 0.022). The **lever rule** is named for the balance: a steel close to the pearlite end must contain mostly pearlite, and the far arm is the long one.

afterFigure.text: It is easy to take the near arm for the share of a phase, but a steel exactly at 0.76 percent carbon shows why that cannot be right, because it is all pearlite and the near arm has length zero. The fraction of ferrite is the other arm over the whole bar, and the two fractions add to 1. The figure shows the rule for steels with 0.20 and 0.50 percent carbon.

diagram.alt: A horizontal bar from ferrite at 0.022 percent carbon to pearlite at 0.76 percent carbon, with a triangle marking the composition of the steel. The arm from ferrite to the steel is highlighted, and its length divided by the whole bar gives the fraction of pearlite.
diagram.caption: The lever rule: the fraction of pearlite is the arm on the ferrite side, divided by the whole bar. Use the buttons to move the steel's carbon content.

steps.headline: Find the fraction of pearlite in a 0.40 percent carbon steel cooled slowly to just below 727 C.

workedSteps.text: The two ends of the bar are ferrite at 0.022 percent carbon and pearlite at 0.76 percent, and the steel sits at 0.40 percent.
The share of pearlite comes from one arm, divided by the whole bar.
Working out the arm and the whole bar gives
Dividing gives the fraction of pearlite, which is about half of the steel.

steps.headline: Find the fraction of pearlite in a 0.60 percent carbon steel cooled slowly to just below 727 C.

workedSteps.text: The steel sits nearer to the pearlite end than the last one, so its pearlite fraction should be larger than 0.512.
The arm on the ferrite side is 0.60 - 0.022 = 0.578, and the whole bar is 0.738. Work out the fraction of pearlite.

steps.headline: Cooling steel too fast for carbon to move gives martensite, and tempering trades some of its hardness for toughness.

lead.text: The pearlite structure needs carbon to move, and it can only do so if the cooling is slow. If austenite is cooled very quickly, for example by plunging it into water or oil, which is called **quenching**, the carbon is caught in the iron lattice, and the lattice shears into a strained structure called **martensite**. The trapped carbon makes dislocations very hard to move, so martensite is far harder and stronger than pearlite, and it is also brittle. A steel as quenched is therefore usually too brittle to use.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is **tempering**: reheating the quenched steel to a temperature well below 727 C, which lets some of the carbon leave the lattice as small carbides. Tempering at 200 C removes a little brittleness and keeps most of the hardness, which suits a chef's knife that must hold an edge. Tempering at 500 C makes the steel tough but softer, which suits parts that have to absorb impact. This is why carbon content and heat treatment can change the strength of one steel severalfold, and the figure shows the four treatments side by side.

diagram.alt: Four cards describing what slow cooling, quenching, tempering at 200 degrees and tempering at 500 degrees do to a hardened steel, with the structure and the hardness and toughness of each.

lead.text: The lever rule can also be run backwards, from the share of pearlite wanted to the carbon content that gives it.

reveal.text: A designer can choose the carbon content to set the proportions of soft ferrite and hard pearlite, and the heat treatment then adjusts them further.

lessons.orientation: Use the iron-carbon diagram's lever rule and say what quenching and tempering do.
lessons.nextAction: Move from metals to polymers, ceramics and composites, and compute a composite's stiffness along and across its fibres.

blocks.text: A chef's knife and a paper clip are both made of steel, and yet one holds a razor edge while the other bends in the fingers. The difference lies in less than one percent of carbon and in how the steel was cooled: the same alloy can come out soft and ductile or hard and brittle, with a strength that varies several times over.

Steel owes this range to a single change in the iron itself. Above 727 C the iron takes a form that can dissolve carbon, and as the steel cools the carbon either has time to leave the iron and gather into a separate compound or is trapped where it is, so the carbon content and the speed of cooling together decide what structure forms. Knowing that, you can work out how much of each structure a slowly cooled steel contains, and see why quenching makes a steel hard and tempering gives back some of its toughness.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to use the lever rule on a slowly cooled steel and say what quenching and tempering do to its structure and its properties.
intro.whyItMatters: Steel is by far the most used engineering metal, and its properties are chosen by carbon content and heat treatment, not by picking a different material.

recap.keyIdea: Slow cooling gives ferrite and pearlite in proportions set by the lever rule, quenching gives hard brittle martensite, and tempering trades some of that hardness for toughness.

blocks.text: Carbon is soluble in austenite and hardly at all in ferrite, so cooling forces it into cementite. Slow cooling gives proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite, in the proportions found by the lever rule from the arm on the far side, as 0.512 pearlite for 0.40 percent carbon, and quenching gives martensite, which tempering softens a controlled amount.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from metals to polymers, ceramics and composites, and to the temperature and direction effects that set them apart.

lessons.title: Polymers, ceramics and composites

steps.headline: A polymer is a network of long chains, and whether the chains are cross-linked decides if it can be melted again.

lead.text: A polymer is made of very long chains of covalently bonded atoms, held to one another by the [[secondary bonds|The weak attractions between chains and molecules. Met in 'Bonds, density and the four families'.]] of the earlier lesson. In a **thermoplastic**, such as the polyethylene of a shopping bag, that is all there is: nothing joins the chains except the weak attractions, so when the polymer is warmed the chains slide past each other, the material softens and flows, and cooling sets it again. A thermoplastic can therefore be melted, shaped and remelted many times.

In a **thermoset** the chains are tied to each other by covalent **cross-links**, so the whole piece is one network. A cured epoxy is a thermoset. Heating cannot let the chains slide, because they are chained together, and a thermoset therefore stays solid until it is hot enough to decompose. A thermoset cannot be melted down and remade, and that is why it is moulded once, while its chemistry is still reacting, rather than after.

afterFigure.text: The cross-links also change the stiffness: the more of them a thermoset has, the stiffer and more brittle it becomes. The next screen shows how both classes respond to temperature, and for that it uses a temperature at which a polymer changes character.

reveal.text: Cross-links are the permanent part of the structure, which is why a thermoset's shape is fixed when it cures.

steps.headline: Below its glass transition temperature a polymer is stiff and glassy, and above it the chains can move and it turns soft.

lead.text: A polymer does not go from solid to liquid at a single temperature. At low temperature the chains are frozen in place and the polymer is hard, stiff and brittle, like glass. As the temperature rises, there is a fairly narrow range, centred on the **glass transition temperature** Tg, in which the chains begin to move and the stiffness drops by a factor of a hundred or more. Polystyrene, with a Tg of about 100 C, is glassy at room temperature, whereas a silicone rubber, with a Tg of about -125 C, is far above its Tg at room temperature and is soft and stretchy.

afterFigure.text: The figure contrasts the two classes. A thermoplastic drops to a soft rubbery state above Tg and then melts and flows at a higher temperature. A thermoset drops less, because its cross-links hold the network together, stays rubbery, and does not melt: it decomposes if heated enough. Knowing Tg therefore tells you the temperature above which a polymer part stops being stiff.

diagram.alt: Two schematic curves of stiffness against temperature on a log scale. A thermoplastic is stiff below its glass transition, drops to a soft rubbery level above it, and melts and flows at a higher temperature. A thermoset drops less at the glass transition, stays solid and rubbery, and chars instead of melting.
diagram.caption: Stiffness against temperature, schematic. The glass transition is where a polymer changes from stiff and glassy to soft and rubbery.

reveal.text: Chilled well below -70 C a rubber band becomes glassy and can snap like a stick of glass, which is why rubber seals fail in extreme cold.

lead.text: The flaws in a ceramic are tiny, often no more than scratches in its surface.

reveal.text: The two loads treat a flaw in opposite ways, and the next screen follows each one in turn.

steps.headline: Ceramics are strong in compression and weak in tension, because surface flaws grow only when they are pulled open.

lead.text: The ionic and covalent bonds of a ceramic resist sliding, so there are no mobile dislocations to blunt a crack, and nothing lets the material yield. A ceramic part is therefore full of small flaws, such as scratches, pores and grain boundaries, and any one of them can start a crack. Under tension the load pulls the flaw open and concentrates stress at its tip, so the crack grows and the part breaks, and it does so at a stress far below what the bonds could carry.

afterFigure.text: Under compression the same flaw is squeezed shut and cannot grow. The material then fails only at a far higher stress, which is why bricks, concrete and thick glass blocks serve in compression. Window glass fails in tension from surface flaws, which is why a scratch lets a pane be snapped along it. Ceramics are not weak in general: tension simply happens to be the one load that their flaws exploit.

diagram.alt: A ceramic block with a small flaw in its top surface. Under tension the load pulls the flaw open and a crack can grow. Under compression the load squeezes the flaw shut.
diagram.caption: The same flaw is dangerous in tension and harmless in compression.

steps.headline: A fibre composite is stiff along its fibres, where the stiffnesses add by volume, and much softer across them, where the matrix controls the result.

lead.text: A composite uses fibres, stiff and strong, to carry load, and a matrix, usually a polymer, to hold them in place. Suppose a composite has fibre volume fraction Vf. Pulled **along** the fibres, fibre and matrix are bonded and must stretch by the same strain, so each carries a stress equal to its own modulus times that strain, and the composite's modulus is E = Vf x Ef + (1 - Vf) x Em. The stiffnesses add in proportion to the volume each part occupies, and the fibres, being so much stiffer, dominate.

afterFigure.text: Pulled **across** the fibres the load passes in series through fibre and matrix, so the stress is the same in both, and it is the compliances 1 / E that add in proportion to volume: 1 / E = Vf / Ef + (1 - Vf) / Em. The soft matrix stretches far more than the fibre, so it controls the result, and a composite is strongly directional. The figure shows both loads, and the next screens put numbers on them.

diagram.alt: A composite plate with four fibre strips running left to right in a matrix. In the first view the load pulls along the fibres, so fibres and matrix stretch by the same strain. In the second the load pulls across the fibres, so the same stress passes through fibre and matrix in turn.
diagram.caption: Fibres run left to right. Pulled along them the composite is stiff. Pulled across them the soft matrix controls the stiffness.

blocks.text: A polyethylene shopping bag softens in hot water and can be melted down and moulded into something new as often as anyone likes, while a cured epoxy glue never melts and, heated enough, simply chars. Both are polymers, long chains of carbon-based molecules, and the difference between them comes down to whether the chains are joined to each other by bonds that heat cannot loosen.

Ceramics and composites are just as strongly shaped by how they are built. A pane of window glass can be broken by a scratch that removes almost none of its material, and a carbon-fibre sheet that is stiffer than steel along its fibres can be floppy across them. Once you can see the structure behind each of these, you can say which polymers can be recycled by melting, why a ceramic is so sensitive to its surface, and how stiff a composite will be in each direction from the stiffness of its fibres and its matrix.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell a thermoplastic from a thermoset, explain what the glass transition and a flaw each do, and compute a composite's stiffness along and across its fibres.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing a polymer, a ceramic or a composite starts with knowing the temperature, the load direction and the flaws it has to live with.

recap.keyIdea: Polymers are set by their chains and cross-links, ceramics by their flaws, and composites by the direction of their fibres.

blocks.text: Thermoplastics can be remelted because their chains are only weakly bonded, and thermosets cannot, because covalent cross-links join the chains into a network. Polymers soften at their glass transition temperature, and ceramics fail in tension because surface flaws open and grow, while in compression they close. A composite along its fibres has a modulus of Vf x Ef + (1 - Vf) x Em, which for carbon fibre in epoxy at 60 percent is 139.2 GPa, and across them 7.36 GPa.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows a crack through a material and asks what stress makes it grow.

lessons.title: Fracture, cracks and toughness

steps.headline: A crack forces the lines of stress to bunch up at its tip, and the stress there depends on the crack length as well as on the load.

lead.text: Imagine a plate pulled in tension. If the plate is whole, the load is shared evenly across it, and the stress is the force divided by the area. A crack changes that, because the load cannot cross it, so the lines of stress that would have passed through the cracked region have to go around, and they crowd together at the tip. The figure shows this for a short and then a longer crack, and the stress at the tip is much larger than the stress applied to the plate.

afterFigure.text: The effect is measured by the **stress intensity** K, which for a crack of length a is K = Y x stress x square root of (pi x a). Here Y is a number near 1 that depends on the shape of the part, and K is in MPa times the square root of metres, with a in metres. Because K grows with the stress and with the square root of the crack length, a larger crack in the same load means a larger K.

diagram.alt: A plate under tension with a crack running in from its left edge. Lines representing the stress crowd together at the tip of the crack. A longer crack has a tip further into the plate and a higher stress at the tip.
diagram.caption: Lines of stress cannot cross the crack, so they bunch up at its tip, where the stress is far above the applied stress. A longer crack makes this worse.

reveal.text: K gives a single number for how severely the crack is loading the material. The next screen compares it with what the material can stand.
The square root makes the effect weaker than a halving, but it still falls quickly, and a crack that grows gradually moves the part towards failure.

steps.headline: A material has a fracture toughness K_IC, and a crack runs when the stress intensity reaches it.

lead.text: Every material can withstand a certain stress intensity before a crack in it grows, and that value is the **fracture toughness** K_IC. Window glass has a K_IC of only about 0.7 MPa sqrt(m), alumina about 4, an aluminium alloy 25 to 40, and a structural steel 50 or more. Ceramics are strong in compression but have little tolerance for a crack, and metals can tolerate a crack of a usable size because they yield at the tip and blunt it.

afterFigure.text: Setting K equal to K_IC and solving gives the two quantities that designers use. The **critical stress** is K_IC divided by (Y x square root of (pi x a)), the stress at which a crack of length a runs, and the **critical crack length** is a = (K_IC / stress)^2 / pi, the longest crack the material tolerates at a given stress. The graph shows the critical stress falling as the crack grows, for three toughness values. A tougher material lifts the whole curve.

diagram.alt: A graph of the stress at which a crack grows against crack length, for toughness values K of 30, 50 and 80 MPa times the square root of metres. Every curve falls as the crack grows, and a tougher material has a higher curve.
diagram.caption: Critical stress falls with the square root of crack length, and a higher toughness lifts the whole curve. K is in MPa times the square root of metres.

steps.headline: Ductile metals blunt a crack by yielding at its tip, and some steels lose this ability when they get cold.

lead.text: The stress at the tip of a crack can rise above the yield strength. In a ductile metal the material there simply yields, forming a **plastic zone** that blunts the tip and absorbs energy, and the crack grows only after much more load has been applied. A ceramic has no such mechanism, because its bonds do not let planes slide, and that is why its fracture toughness is so low. Between the two sits the temperature, which can switch a steel from one behaviour to the other.

afterFigure.text: Low-carbon steels have a **ductile-brittle transition**: above a certain temperature range they yield and absorb a great deal of energy before they break, and below it the plastic zone disappears and a crack runs across the section with little energy. Welded Liberty ships built in the early 1940s cracked in cold seas in just this way, and some broke in two, which is why impact tests at low temperature became standard for ship steels. Aluminium alloys and austenitic stainless steels have no such transition, as the figure shows.

diagram.alt: Two curves of the energy absorbed in fracture against temperature. Low-carbon steel absorbs little energy when cold, rises steeply through a narrow transition range and absorbs a lot when warm. An aluminium alloy absorbs a high energy at every temperature.
diagram.caption: The energy a steel absorbs in fracture can fall by a large factor over a narrow temperature range. Schematic, with no values on the axes.

reveal.text: The practical test is an impact test at several temperatures, with the steel chosen so that the transition lies well below the lowest working temperature.

lead.text: A designer replaces a steel with K_IC = 50 MPa sqrt(m), working at 400 MPa, by a stronger but less tough steel that is allowed to work at a higher stress.

reveal.text: Stronger steels often have lower toughness, so a higher strength can mean a smaller tolerable crack. This is why inspection is set by the critical crack length, not by the yield strength.

lessons.orientation: Compute the stress at which a crack of given size grows and say why brittle fracture surprises.
lessons.nextAction: Look at corrosion, the other slow way that sound metal fails, and see how it works as an electrochemical cell.

blocks.text: A part made of a strong steel and carrying a stress well below its yield strength can still fail suddenly if it holds a crack, because the stress at the tip of a crack is far above the stress in the rest of the part. A scratch in a pane of glass works the same way on a small scale, since the glass itself is as strong as it was and the scratch only gives the load a place to concentrate.

How much the stress concentrates depends on the length of the crack, which is why a crack that was harmless when it was found can fail a structure once it has grown. Fracture mechanics puts a number on this, so that for a given material you can work out the stress at which a crack of known length will run, or the longest crack a part can carry at its working stress.

diagram.alt: A plate under tension with a crack running in from its left edge. Lines representing the stress crowd together at the tip of the crack. A longer crack has a tip further into the plate and a higher stress at the tip.
diagram.caption: Lines of stress cannot cross the crack, so they bunch up at its tip, where the stress is far above the applied stress. A longer crack makes this worse.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the critical stress for a crack of a given length, find the critical crack length for a given stress, and explain why steels get brittle when cold.
intro.whyItMatters: Fractures with no warning are the ones that cost most, and this lesson shows how to calculate when a crack will run.

recap.keyIdea: A crack runs when K = Y x stress x square root of (pi x a) reaches the material's K_IC, so critical stress falls as the square root of crack length.

blocks.text: A crack concentrates stress at its tip, and it runs when the stress intensity K reaches the fracture toughness K_IC, which gives a critical stress K_IC / (Y sqrt(pi a)) and a critical crack length (K_IC / stress)^2 / pi. Ductile metals blunt the tip by yielding, but steels lose this below their ductile-brittle transition, and a stronger steel can have a lower toughness.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at corrosion, a different way for a sound part to lose its strength over time.

lessons.title: Corrosion

steps.headline: Corrosion is an electrochemical cell, and it needs an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte and a metal path between them.

lead.text: Rusting is often described as iron reacting with oxygen in the air, but air alone does nothing to a dry steel part. What damages it is a small electrochemical cell, with four parts. At the **anode** the iron atoms give up electrons and dissolve into the water as Fe2+ ions. The electrons travel through the steel to the **cathode**, where oxygen takes them up and forms hydroxide ions. The water with its dissolved salts, the **electrolyte**, carries ions between the two, and the metal itself provides the path for the electrons.

afterFigure.text: Take any one of these away and the cell stops, which is why dry steel does not rust and why salt water, a better electrolyte, speeds it up. Metal is lost only at the anode. The cathode is where oxygen is used up, and the metal there does not dissolve. The figure shows a drop of salt water on steel, with its centre as the anode, and then the same steel dry.

diagram.alt: A drop of salt water on a steel surface. The centre of the drop is the anode, where iron dissolves as ions and releases electrons, and the edge is the cathode, where oxygen takes up electrons. A second view shows dry steel with no drop and no corrosion cell.
diagram.caption: A corrosion cell needs an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte and a metal path between them. Dry steel has no electrolyte.

reveal.text: The metal is therefore lost wherever the anode happens to form, and it can be a pit in a surface that looks sound elsewhere.
Which metal loses material depends on which is more willing to give up electrons, as the next screen explains.

steps.headline: When two metals touch in an electrolyte, the more active one becomes the anode and corrodes, and the less active one is protected.

lead.text: Metals differ in how readily they give up electrons, and the standard electrode potential puts a number on it: the more negative the potential, the more active the metal. Magnesium is at -2.37 V, aluminium at -1.66 V, zinc at -0.76 V, iron at -0.44 V and copper at +0.34 V. Joined in a wet joint, the more negative metal becomes the anode of the cell and loses metal, while the other becomes the cathode and is protected. Zinc protects steel, aluminium corrodes next to steel, and steel corrodes next to copper.

afterFigure.text: Two further points matter in practice. A small anode joined to a large cathode corrodes faster, because the whole current is concentrated on a small area, which is why small aluminium rivets in a large steel plate are a poor design. And the nobler metal is not damaged: the cathode is protected, though its partner pays for that. The figure shows three pairs with steel.

diagram.alt: A ladder of standard electrode potentials: magnesium minus 2.37 volts, aluminium minus 1.66, zinc minus 0.76, iron minus 0.44 and copper plus 0.34. In each view two metals are joined. The one lower on the ladder, with the more negative potential, is the anode and corrodes.
diagram.caption: In a pair of joined metals the one with the more negative potential is the anode and corrodes. Use the buttons to change the partner of steel.

steps.headline: Faraday's law links the current through a corrosion cell to the mass of metal it removes.

lead.text: Each atom that dissolves gives up n electrons, so the amount of metal lost is fixed by the charge that flows. A current I flowing for a time t carries a charge I x t, and each mole of electrons carries 96,485 coulombs, the Faraday constant F. Dividing the charge by n x F gives the moles of metal lost, and multiplying by the molar mass M gives the mass: m = I x t x M / (n x F). The number n is the charge on the ion that the metal forms as it dissolves.

afterFigure.text: The result is often surprisingly large. Copper dissolves as Cu2+, so n is 2, and its molar mass is 63.55 g/mol. A steady current of only 0.05 A, which is 50 mA, flowing for 30 days, or 2.592 x 10^6 seconds, removes 0.05 x 2.592e6 x 63.55 / (2 x 96485), about 42.7 g of copper. A small corrosion current therefore costs a large mass over time, and the next screens apply the formula to iron and zinc.

The charge is 0.02 x 3.156e7 coulombs. Put it into the formula and work out the mass lost.

steps.headline: Protection works by keeping the electrolyte out, or by making another metal the anode.

lead.text: There are three ways to keep a metal part from corroding. The first is a **barrier**: paint, plastic or enamel keeps water off the metal, and it works as long as the layer is whole. A scratch exposes bare steel, and the corrosion there can spread underneath the coating. The second is a **sacrificial** coating. **Galvanising** covers steel with zinc, which is more active than iron, so that even where the zinc is scratched the zinc is the anode and the exposed steel is the cathode. The third is a sacrificial anode, a block of zinc or magnesium bolted on and replaced when it is used up.

afterFigure.text: Design helps too: keeping dissimilar metals apart, or insulating them from each other, stops a galvanic cell from forming, and letting water drain from a joint removes the electrolyte. Stainless steels resist corrosion because chromium forms a thin, tough oxide film that stops the reaction. The figure compares a scratched paint layer and a scratched zinc coating.

diagram.alt: Cross-sections of a steel plate with a scratch through its coating. With paint, the steel exposed in the scratch rusts and the rust spreads under the paint. With a zinc coating, the zinc is the anode, so it corrodes in preference to the exposed steel, which stays protected.
diagram.caption: A paint is a barrier and a zinc coating is a sacrificial layer. They behave differently once scratched.

lead.text: Faraday's law can be turned round to give the time needed to lose a given mass.

reveal.text: Rearranging the formula for the quantity you need is the usual use of it: how long a sacrificial anode lasts is found in the same way.

lessons.orientation: Explain corrosion as a cell, predict galvanic pairs, and compute metal loss from current.
lessons.nextAction: Move from what materials are to how things are made, starting with casting and the time a casting takes to freeze.

blocks.text: A steady current of only 0.01 A, which is 10 mA and about enough to make a small LED glow faintly, would remove roughly 91 g of iron from a steel structure in a year if it flowed through a corrosion cell. Rust forms because a wet metal surface becomes a small electrical cell, and the metal it loses can be measured and calculated from the current like any other quantity in a circuit.

Seeing corrosion as a cell explains why the rules for preventing it are so specific. Which metal touches which decides which of the two dissolves, water on the surface completes the circuit, and a scratch in a coating does more or less harm depending on the metal the coating is made of, so each rule follows from the way the cell is built, and the current tells you how fast the metal goes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the parts of a corrosion cell, decide which metal of a pair corrodes, compute the mass of metal lost from a current, and choose a protection.
intro.whyItMatters: Corrosion decides how long a metal part lasts in service, and it can be prevented once its mechanism is known.

recap.keyIdea: Corrosion is a cell in which the more active metal is the anode and loses mass in proportion to the charge that flows, so protection makes the anode something else.

blocks.text: Corrosion needs an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte and a metal path, and the more active metal of a pair is the anode, which is why zinc protects steel and steel corrodes beside copper. Faraday's law, m = I x t x M / (n x F), gives the metal lost, about 91.3 g of iron a year at 0.01 A. Paint only keeps the electrolyte out, whereas zinc and sacrificial anodes change which metal is the anode.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson begins the making half of the course with casting, and the time a casting takes to freeze.

lessons.title: Casting

steps.headline: A casting freezes from its outside inward, and the last part to freeze is where the shrinkage hole forms unless a riser is placed there.

lead.text: In casting, liquid metal is poured into a mould cavity that has the shape of the part. The cavity is made by packing sand around a **pattern**, a replica of the part, which is then removed. The metal runs down a channel called the sprue into the cavity, and it loses heat to the mould and freezes. Metal also gets smaller as it cools and freezes, so a casting that freezes with no further supply of liquid ends up with a hole in the last place to freeze.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is a **riser**, a reservoir of liquid metal attached to the casting. It is designed to freeze *after* the casting, so that it can feed liquid metal into the casting while the casting shrinks, and the shrinkage hole forms in the riser, which is later cut away. The figure follows a casting from pouring to the end of freezing. To size a riser, and to know how long a casting will take to freeze, a rule for freezing time is needed.

diagram.alt: A cross-section of a sand mould with a vertical sprue, a horizontal casting cavity and a riser rising above the cavity. In the first view liquid metal fills everything. In the second the casting has frozen and the riser is still liquid. In the third all of it has frozen, with a shrink hole at the top of the riser.
diagram.caption: The casting freezes first and the riser last, so the shrinkage hole ends up in the riser instead of the casting.

reveal.text: A thicker section has a larger V / A. It has more metal for each square millimetre of surface to lose heat through, and it therefore takes longer.
The time does not simply double. The next screen gives the rule that governs it.

steps.headline: Freezing time is proportional to the square of the volume to surface area ratio, so a casting twice as thick takes four times as long.

lead.text: The rule, known as **Chvorinov's rule**, is t = B x (V / A)^2, where B is a constant that depends on the mould material and the metal. The square matters. A cube of side 100 mm has V / A of 16.7 mm, and a cube of 50 mm has 8.33 mm, so the smaller cube freezes in (1 / 2)^2 = one quarter of the time. Because the time goes with the square, a casting twice as thick freezes in four times as long, even though it holds only about twice as much metal in the thickness direction.

afterFigure.text: For a cube, V / A is simply the side divided by 6, and for any shape it is found by dividing the volume by the area of the surface that touches the mould. Two parts of the same casting can have very different values, and thin parts freeze long before thick ones, which is why a good casting has an even thickness. The figure compares the two cubes drawn to scale.

diagram.alt: Two cubes of the same metal drawn to scale, one with side 100 mm and one with side 50 mm. The large cube has a volume to area ratio of 16.7 millimetres and the small one 8.33 millimetres, so the small cube freezes in one quarter of the time.
diagram.caption: Halving every dimension halves V / A, and the freezing time falls to one quarter.

steps.headline: Metal shrinks as it cools, so the pattern must be larger than the casting by an allowance.

lead.text: A casting shrinks in three stages: the liquid contracts as it cools, it contracts again as it freezes, and the solid contracts as it cools to room temperature. The riser takes care of the first two by feeding liquid. The third is a change in size of the whole casting, and the **shrinkage allowance** covers it: the pattern is made larger than the casting wanted, so that the casting shrinks to the right size.

afterFigure.text: The allowance is a percentage of the pattern, so the pattern length is the casting length divided by (1 - s), where s is the fraction that the metal shrinks. A casting that must be 735 mm long, in a metal that shrinks 2 percent, needs a pattern of 735 / 0.98 = 750 mm. A common mistake is to add 2 percent to 735, which gives 749.7 mm and leaves the casting slightly small, though in practice the difference is a matter of tolerance.

reveal.text: Pattern makers also add allowances for machining, for draft and for distortion, but the shrinkage allowance is usually the largest.

steps.headline: The choice between sand casting and die casting is a choice between cheap tooling and cheap parts.

lead.text: In **sand casting** the mould is made from sand around a pattern and is broken up to remove the part, so every casting needs a new mould. The tooling, a pattern, is cheap, so the process suits one-off parts and runs up to thousands, and it can cast large pieces and high-melting metals such as iron and steel. Its surface finish and tolerance are rougher. In **die casting** liquid metal is forced into a steel mould, a die, that can be used many times. The die costs a great deal, but each part then costs little and comes out accurate, which suits aluminium and zinc in runs of thousands to millions.

afterFigure.text: The same pattern appears throughout manufacturing: a high cost paid once, as tooling, against a lower cost paid with every part. The cards compare the two processes, and a later lesson computes the volume at which tooling pays back.

diagram.alt: Two cards comparing sand casting and die casting by mould, tooling cost, number of parts and surface finish.
diagram.caption: Sand casting spends little on the mould and much on each part, and die casting spends heavily on tooling and little per part.

blocks.text: A cube of metal 100 mm on a side holds eight times the metal of a cube 50 mm on a side, but its surface is only four times as large. Metal in a mould loses its heat through its surface, so the time a casting takes to freeze is set by how much metal lies behind each square millimetre of that surface, the ratio of volume to surface area, and for the larger cube that ratio is twice as large.

The rule that links this ratio to the freezing time is Chvorinov's rule, and foundries depend on it. Metal shrinks as it freezes, and the part of a casting that freezes last is left with a hole unless liquid metal can still reach it, so a reservoir of extra metal has to be attached that freezes after the casting does. With the rule you can compare the freezing times of two shapes and size that reservoir so that it is the last thing to freeze.

intro.whyItMatters: Casting is one of the oldest ways of shaping metal, and it is still the cheapest way to make a large or complex part.

recap.keyIdea: Freezing time is B x (V / A)^2, so a riser must have a larger V / A than the casting, and the pattern must be bigger than the casting by the shrinkage allowance.

blocks.text: A casting loses heat through its surface, so its freezing time is B x (V / A)^2, and a casting twice as thick takes four times as long. The riser has to have the larger V / A so that it freezes last and takes the shrinkage hole with it. The pattern is the casting length divided by (1 - s), 750 mm for a 735 mm casting with 2 percent shrinkage, and the process is chosen by weighing tooling cost against cost per part.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shapes metal without melting it, by forging, rolling and bending.

lessons.title: Forging, rolling and bending

steps.headline: In forming, metal is reshaped by plastic deformation without changing its volume, so a shorter piece must be wider.

lead.text: Forming shapes solid metal by pushing it past its yield point. In **forging** the metal is squeezed between dies, in **rolling** it is passed between rollers that make it thinner and longer, and in **bending** a sheet is deformed around a tool. All of them have one thing in common: plastic deformation moves the metal about without making any of it vanish, so the volume stays constant. When a billet is squeezed to half its height, as in the figure, the area it covers doubles.

afterFigure.text: This is the fact that links the next ideas. It makes the strain independent of the shape of the part, since the heights, lengths and widths of the part change together. It also explains why the force needed to forge a billet grows as the billet flattens, and why a forged piece can be made in a shape that no amount of cutting would get from the same bar without waste.

diagram.alt: A metal billet squeezed between two flat dies. Before, it is 50 mm tall with a cross-section of 2000 mm2. After, it is 25 mm tall with a cross-section of 4000 mm2. Both have a volume of 100,000 mm3.
diagram.caption: Plastic deformation does not change the volume. A shorter billet must be wider, so its area grows. Use the buttons to compare.
