reveal.text: The new area is more than twice the old one, because the billet has been flattened to well under half of its height.
The percentages do not simply add, and the next screen gives a measure of strain that does.

steps.headline: True strain is the natural logarithm of the ratio of lengths, and unlike percentages it adds from one pass to the next.

lead.text: Engineering strain compares a change in length with the *original* length, and so every pass of a rolling operation uses a different reference. The **true strain** avoids this by adding up small steps, each measured against the length at that moment, and the sum is ln(L1 / L0). For a plate rolled thinner, the same formula holds with thicknesses, ln(h0 / h1), with the larger starting thickness on top. A reduction from 20 mm to 15 mm has a true strain of ln(20 / 15) = 0.288.

afterFigure.text: Its great advantage is that true strains add. Rolling 20 mm to 15 mm and then to 10 mm gives 0.288 + 0.405 = 0.693, which is ln(20 / 10), the strain of reducing 20 mm to 10 mm in one pass. The percentage reductions, 25 and 33.3, would suggest 58.3 percent, but the real reduction is 50 percent. The figure shows both ways of counting.

steps.headline: The force to forge a part is the flow stress times the contact area, and the area grows as the part flattens.

lead.text: Once a metal is yielding, the stress needed to keep it deforming is its **flow stress**, which is close to its yield strength and rises as it work hardens. The force needed to squeeze a billet is the flow stress times the area of the billet in contact with the dies, so a flow stress of 250 MPa on an area of 2000 mm2 needs 250 x 2000 = 500,000 N, or 500 kN, because 1 MPa is 1 N per mm2. Friction at the dies adds to this, so 500 kN is a minimum.

Since the volume is constant, the force rises as the billet flattens: when the height halves and the area doubles, as in the figure at the start of the lesson, the force doubles too, to 1000 kN at the same flow stress. A press must therefore be chosen for the force at the *end* of the stroke. The flow stress is lower when the metal is hot, which is the main reason for forging steel at 1100 to 1250 C.

reveal.text: The forces involved in forging are large, which is why presses and hammers are some of the heaviest machines in a factory.

steps.headline: Hot working keeps a metal soft by recrystallising it as it deforms, and cold working hardens it.

lead.text: Whether the metal hardens as it is formed depends on its temperature. Above the **recrystallisation temperature**, roughly half the melting point on the kelvin scale, new strain-free grains form as fast as deformation creates dislocations, so the metal stays soft and its flow stress is low. This is **hot working**. Below it, the dislocations pile up as in the work hardening of the earlier lesson, so the metal gets stronger and less ductile, and this is **cold working**.

afterFigure.text: Each has its uses. Hot working takes much less force and allows large changes of shape in one go, but the surface oxidises and the dimensions are loose. Cold working gives a good surface and close tolerances, and it makes the part stronger, but it takes more force and has a limit to the strain before the metal cracks. Annealing can restore ductility between stages, and many parts are hot worked to shape and then finished cold.

reveal.text: The flow stress of hot steel is a fraction of its room-temperature value, so a smaller press can do the same job.

steps.headline: A bend needs a flat length equal to its neutral axis arc, and the part springs back a little when the tool is removed.

lead.text: When a sheet is bent, the outer face stretches and the inner face is squeezed, and somewhere between them a layer keeps its original length. That layer is the **neutral axis**, and it sits at a distance K x t from the inner face, where t is the thickness and K a number near 0.33 to 0.5 found from tables. The length of flat sheet used up in the bend, the **bend allowance**, is the length of the neutral axis arc: (angle in radians) x (R + K x t), where R is the inner radius.

afterFigure.text: For a 90 degree bend, with R = 3 mm, t = 2 mm and K = 0.33, the neutral axis is at 3 + 0.66 = 3.66 mm and the allowance is (pi / 2) x 3.66 = 5.75 mm. Removing the tool does not leave the bend where it was: some of the strain was elastic and it recovers, so the bend opens by a few degrees. This is **springback**, and it is allowed for by bending a little past the target angle.

diagram.alt: A sheet of metal bent through 90 degrees. The inner radius is 3 mm, the thickness 2 mm, and a dashed neutral axis sits 3.66 mm from the centre of the bend. A second view shows the bent part opening slightly after the load is removed.
diagram.caption: The neutral axis keeps its length when the sheet is bent, so the flat length needed for the bend is the length of that arc. The second view shows springback.

blocks.text: A billet, a short solid block of metal, 50 mm tall and squeezed in a press to half that height, loses no metal, so it has to get wider instead: the area it covers doubles, and because the press has to push on all of that area, the force needed to keep squeezing it doubles too. That plastic deformation keeps the volume constant is the fact behind most of the arithmetic of metal forming.

Because no metal appears or disappears, forming comes down to tracking how a part's dimensions trade against each other as it is reshaped. That lets you work out the force a press must supply as the part spreads under it, the strain a plate takes on over a series of rolling passes, and the length of flat sheet that a bend uses up.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute true strain, forging force and the allowance for a sheet bend, and to tell hot working from cold working.
intro.whyItMatters: These are the quantities a manufacturer needs to size a press, plan a rolling schedule or cut a sheet blank.

recap.keyIdea: Volume is constant in forming, true strain ln(L1 / L0) adds across passes, forging force is flow stress times area, and bends use the neutral axis arc.

blocks.text: Plastic deformation keeps the volume constant, so squeezing a billet widens it, and the force, flow stress times area, rises as it flattens. True strain, ln(L1 / L0), adds from pass to pass where percentages do not. A bend takes a flat length of (angle in radians) x (R + K x t) and springs back a little, and hot working above about half the melting point keeps the metal soft where cold working hardens it.

lessons.title: Machining

steps.headline: Turning is set by three quantities: cutting speed, feed and depth of cut.

lead.text: On a lathe the workpiece turns while a tool cuts a chip from its surface. The surface of a bar of diameter D, turning at N revolutions per minute, passes the tool at the **cutting speed** v = pi x D x N / 1000 metres per minute, because the surface travels pi x D millimetres in each turn. A bar 50 mm across turning at 600 rev/min therefore has a surface speed of 94.2 m/min, and it is this speed, and not the rev/min, that governs how hot the edge gets.

afterFigure.text: The tool also advances along the bar. The **feed** f is the distance it advances in each revolution, in mm per revolution, and the **depth of cut** d is how far into the surface it cuts, in mm. Feed and speed are easily confused, since both are called a speed in the workshop, but one is a distance per revolution and the other a distance per minute. The two figures show how each quantity looks on the part.

diagram.alt: Two views of turning on a lathe. In an end view a workpiece of diameter D turns at N revolutions per minute, which gives a cutting speed at its surface. In a side view the tool advances a feed f in each revolution and cuts to a depth d.
diagram.caption: Turning has three settings: the speed of the surface, the feed per revolution and the depth of cut.

steps.headline: The material removal rate is speed times feed times depth, and the power needed is the removal rate times the energy per unit volume.

lead.text: The chip that the tool cuts has a cross-section of f x d, and it is cut at the speed v, so the volume of metal removed each minute is the **material removal rate**, MRR = v x f x d. Using v in mm/min, a speed of 94,250 mm/min with f = 0.2 mm and d = 2 mm removes 94,250 x 0.2 x 2 = 37,700 mm3/min, which is 37.7 cm3/min or 628 mm3/s.

afterFigure.text: Cutting takes energy, and each material needs a fixed amount of it to remove a cubic millimetre, the **specific cutting energy**. At 3 J/mm3, a removal rate of 628 mm3/s needs 3 x 628 = 1885 W, about 1.9 kW. Doubling either the feed or the depth doubles the removal rate and the power, as the figure shows for three feeds.

diagram.alt: Two bar charts for turning at a speed of 94.25 m/min and a depth of cut of 2 mm, at feeds of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 mm per revolution. Material removal rate is 18.9, 37.7 and 75.4 cm3 per minute, and power at 3 J/mm3 is 0.94, 1.88 and 3.77 kW.
diagram.caption: Doubling the feed doubles both the material removed each minute and the power needed.

lead.text: Raising the cutting speed removes metal faster, so each part is finished sooner.

reveal.text: The edge gets hotter, and wear depends strongly on temperature, so the next screen gives a rule that quantifies the loss.

steps.headline: Tool life falls very steeply as cutting speed rises, following Taylor's equation.

lead.text: The cutting edge wears away, and the time T that it lasts before it has to be replaced depends on the cutting speed through **Taylor's equation**, v x T^n = C, where n and C are constants for the tool and the material. For a typical carbide tool n is about 0.25. Rearranged, the life varies as speed to the power -1 / n, which is -4, so a rise in speed by a ratio of 1.2 changes the life by a factor of 1.2^-4 = 0.48.

afterFigure.text: That is a loss of more than half the life for a rise of a fifth in speed. Cutting faster therefore does not reduce the cost per part by the same proportion, since the cost of worn tools, and of the time to change them, rises faster than the output. A smaller exponent n makes the effect still more severe, as the second curve shows, and a part is cheapest to make at a speed well below the fastest the tool can stand.

diagram.alt: Two curves of relative tool life against relative cutting speed, for Taylor exponents of 0.25 and 0.1. In both, tool life falls steeply as speed rises. At 20 percent more speed the life is 0.48 of the original for n = 0.25 and 0.16 for n = 0.1.

reveal.text: A rise of 10 percent in speed costs about a third of the tool's life.
Slowing down buys a large increase in tool life, and the best speed is a balance between the cost of time and the cost of tools.

steps.headline: The theoretical roughness of a turned surface depends on the feed and the nose radius of the tool, and not on the cutting speed.

lead.text: A tool with a rounded tip, of nose radius r, leaves a series of small ridges on the surface, one for each revolution, and their height depends on how far the tool advances between ridges. The theoretical average roughness is Ra = f^2 / (32 r), with f and r in mm. A feed of 0.3 mm/rev and a nose radius of 1.2 mm give 0.09 / 38.4 = 0.00234 mm, which is 2.34 micrometres.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the speed does not appear. The finish improves by *quartering* when the feed is halved, since the feed is squared, and it improves with a larger nose radius, though a large radius can make the tool **chatter**, vibrating against the work and marking it. Real surfaces are rougher than the theoretical value, but this is the target a finishing cut is set to reach.

reveal.text: The answer is in millimetres, so it has to be multiplied by 1000 to give micrometres.
A finishing pass uses a small feed for this reason, although the part then takes longer to cut.

lessons.orientation: Calculate cutting speed, material-removal rate, cutting power and the effect of speed on tool life.
lessons.nextAction: Compare moulding, printing and machining by what each costs per part and per tool.

blocks.text: A bar 50 mm across, turning at 600 revolutions a minute, drags its surface past a cutting tool at 94.2 metres a minute. The tool takes a chip 0.2 mm wide in feed and 2 mm deep, which is 628 cubic millimetres of metal every second, and the cutting takes about 1.9 kW. Those numbers come from three settings of the machine, and a fourth number, the life of the tool, depends on them more steeply than any of the others.

Machining is the most flexible way to make a precise part, and its economics are set by exactly these quantities. From the three settings you can work out how fast metal is removed and how much power that takes, how long a tool will last when the speed is changed, and what surface finish a given feed will leave.

diagram.alt: Two views of turning on a lathe. In an end view a workpiece of diameter D turns at N revolutions per minute, which gives a cutting speed at its surface. In a side view the tool advances a feed f in each revolution and cuts to a depth d.
diagram.caption: Turning has three settings: the speed of the surface, the feed per revolution and the depth of cut.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute cutting speed, material removal rate and cutting power, and say how a change in speed or feed changes tool life and surface finish.
intro.whyItMatters: Machining sets the cost and the tolerance of most precision parts, and its calculations are simple once the units are kept straight.

recap.keyIdea: Cutting speed is pi x D x N / 1000, removal rate is v x f x d, power is that rate times specific energy, and tool life falls as speed to the power -1 / n.

blocks.text: The cutting speed of a turned bar is pi x D x N / 1000, and with the feed and depth it gives the removal rate v x f x d and, with the specific energy, the cutting power. Tool life falls as speed to the power -1 / n, so a 20 percent rise in speed roughly halves it, and the theoretical roughness f^2 / (32 r) depends on feed and nose radius alone.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson compares moulding, printing and machining by cost, and finds the volume at which tooling pays back.

lessons.title: Moulding, printing and cost per part

steps.headline: Injection moulding forces molten plastic into a closed mould, and the clamp has to hold the mould shut against the pressure.

lead.text: In **injection moulding** plastic granules are melted and forced under high pressure into a closed steel mould, where the plastic cools and sets. The mould then opens and pins eject the part, and the cycle repeats, in a few seconds for small parts. The figure follows one cycle. The process makes the plastic parts of most consumer goods, and it is the cheapest way to make them in large numbers.

afterFigure.text: The injected plastic pushes on the walls of the cavity with a pressure of tens of megapascals, and the two halves of the mould would be forced apart if they were not held. The **clamp force** needed is the cavity pressure times the **projected area**, the area of the part seen in the direction in which the mould opens. At 50 MPa on 10,000 mm2, the force is 50 x 10,000 = 500,000 N, or 500 kN, since 1 MPa is 1 N per mm2.

diagram.alt: Three stages of injection moulding drawn as a cross-section: hot plastic injected into the closed mould while a clamp force holds the halves together, the plastic cooling and setting, and the mould opening to eject the part.
diagram.caption: The cycle repeats every few seconds to a minute. The clamp has to hold the mould shut against the pressure of the injected plastic.

reveal.text: Machines are sold by their clamp force in tonnes or kilonewtons, and the choice of machine follows from this calculation.

steps.headline: A mould has a high cost paid once and a low cost per part, and 3D printing has no tooling but the same cost on every part.

lead.text: Making a part by injection moulding costs two kinds of money. The mould, the **tooling**, is paid for once and can cost tens of thousands of dollars. After that each part costs only the plastic and the machine time, perhaps 1.50. Printing a part needs no tooling, but every part costs the same, say 12, whether it is the first or the thousandth.

afterFigure.text: So the total cost is the tooling plus the cost per part times the number of parts, and the average cost per part is the tooling divided by the number of parts plus the cost per part. Printing is therefore cheap for a few parts, since there is nothing to pay in advance, and moulding is cheap for a large number, since the tooling is shared. It is easy to say that moulding is cheap per part, but it only is once there are enough parts.

reveal.text: The comparison depends on the quantity, and the next screen finds the quantity at which the two totals are equal.

steps.headline: The break-even volume is the tooling cost divided by the saving on each part.

lead.text: Moulding and printing cost the same when 20,000 + 1.50 n = 12 n, where n is the number of parts. Collecting the terms gives 20,000 = (12 - 1.50) n, so the **break-even volume** is n = 20,000 / 10.50 = 1905 parts. Each moulded part saves 10.50 dollars against a printed one, and the tooling is paid back when those savings reach 20,000.

afterFigure.text: The first graph shows the two total costs, which cross at 1905 parts: below it the printed line is lower, and above it the moulded line is. The second shows the cost per part, with the moulded curve falling towards 1.50 as the tooling is spread over more parts. The formula to remember is break-even volume = tooling cost / (cost per part by the other process minus cost per part by moulding).

workedSteps.text: The saving per part is 5.80 - 0.80 = 5.00 dollars.
Divide the tooling cost by this saving to find the break-even volume.

steps.headline: The quantity wanted decides the process: no tooling for a handful, a mould for thousands.

lead.text: The break-even calculation turns into a rule of thumb. For a handful of parts, printing or machining wins because they carry no tooling cost, and their flat cost per part is cheap against any mould. For thousands or millions of parts, injection moulding wins, because the tooling is shared out so thinly that it hardly shows. In between, the answer depends on the cost of the tooling and on how much each process saves per part, which is just what the break-even volume measures.

afterFigure.text: The boundary moves with the numbers. A simple part with a cheap mould breaks even at a few hundred parts, and a complex part with a mould of several hundred thousand dollars may not do so until it passes a hundred thousand. Printing also allows shapes that no mould could release, and the cards below set out the usual choices.

reveal.text: Break-even is proportional to the tooling cost, so one pricey quotation can move a project from moulding to printing.

steps.headline: A moulded part needs draft on its walls and an even wall thickness, because of the way it comes out of the mould and cools.

lead.text: Moulded parts have to be released from a steel mould, so every wall that runs in the direction in which the mould opens is given a slight taper called **draft**, typically between half a degree and two degrees. Without it the walls rub along the mould, and the part sticks or scratches. Draft moves the face of a wall by height x tan(angle): a draft of 1 degree on a wall 40 mm tall moves the face by 40 x tan(1 degree) = 0.70 mm.

afterFigure.text: The wall thickness should also be even. A thick section cools more slowly than a thin one, by the same reasoning that gave a freezing time depending on the square of V / A in casting, so it shrinks later and pulls a dimple, a sink mark, into the surface, or warps the part. Designers hollow out thick regions and use ribs instead, so that every section cools at about the same rate.

diagram.alt: A moulded part in section. With no draft its walls are vertical and rub against the mould as it is ejected. With draft its walls lean slightly so that the part clears the mould at once. The lean in the drawing is exaggerated.
diagram.caption: A small taper on every wall that is parallel to the opening direction lets the part come out cleanly.

lessons.reviewLabel: Moulding, printing and cost per part
lessons.nextAction: Look at tolerances and how often a process stays inside them, with Cp and Cpk.

blocks.text: A mould for a small plastic part can cost 20,000 dollars, after which each moulded part costs about 1.50, while the same part can be printed for 12 dollars with no mould at all. For a handful of parts printing is plainly cheaper and for a million moulding is, so somewhere between the two the total costs must be equal.

That crossing point follows from one line of algebra, and the same calculation applies to any cost paid once before the first part is made, such as a die or a pattern, set against a cost paid on every part. With it you can say which process suits a run of a given size, and how the answer moves when the tooling turns out dearer or the parts cheaper than planned.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute an injection-moulding clamp force, find the volume at which tooling pays back, and say when each process fits.
intro.whyItMatters: Most manufacturing decisions come down to a fixed cost against a cost per part, and the break-even volume says where the choice changes.

recap.keyIdea: Clamp force is cavity pressure times projected area, and tooling pays back at the break-even volume, tooling cost divided by the saving per part.

blocks.text: The clamp must hold the mould against the cavity pressure over the projected area, which for 10,000 mm2 at 50 MPa is 500 kN. Moulding has a high cost paid at the start and a low cost per part, so it beats printing only beyond the break-even volume, tooling cost divided by the saving per part, which was 1905 parts for 20,000 dollars of tooling. Good moulded parts have draft on their walls and an even thickness.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how many of the parts that a process makes will actually meet the tolerance.

lessons.title: Holding tolerance in production

steps.headline: No process makes every part the same, and a tolerance is met only if the spread of the process fits inside it.

lead.text: Machine the same diameter on a thousand parts and the measurements will differ slightly, in a pattern that is close to a normal distribution. It has a mean, which is where the process is aimed or has drifted to, and a standard deviation **sigma**, which is the typical distance from the mean. About 99.73 percent of the parts lie within 3 sigma of the mean, so the whole range of a process covers about 6 sigma. The drawing specifies a **tolerance**, with a **lower specification limit** (LSL) and an **upper specification limit** (USL), and a part is good if it lies between them.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows two processes aimed at 25.00 mm with limits at 24.95 and 25.05 mm. A process with sigma = 0.01 mm has its limits 5 sigma from the mean, and almost nothing falls outside. A process with sigma = 0.02 mm has them only 2.5 sigma away, and about 1.2 percent of parts fall outside, shown in the warm colour. Note that the tolerance and sigma are different quantities: one is what the customer wants, the other is what the process does.

diagram.alt: Two bell curves of the diameter of machined parts, centred on 25.00 mm, with lower and upper specification limits at 24.95 and 25.05 mm. The narrow curve, with a standard deviation of 0.01 mm, sits almost wholly inside the limits. The wide curve, with 0.02 mm, spills over both limits.
diagram.caption: Both processes aim at 25.00 mm. The narrow one fits inside the limits and the wide one does not. Shaded in warm colour is the part of the output that falls outside the limits.

reveal.text: Four sigma is a long way out: about 32 parts in a million fall beyond it.

steps.headline: The Cp index compares the width of the tolerance range with the 6 sigma spread of the process.

lead.text: Dividing the tolerance range by the spread of the process gives a single number, the **process capability index** Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 sigma). For limits of 24.95 and 25.05 mm, the range is 0.10 mm, and with sigma = 0.01 mm the spread is 0.06 mm, so Cp = 0.10 / 0.06 = 1.67. A Cp of 1 means the spread of the process just fills the tolerance, with no margin at all, and a value above 1 means the spread fits inside with room to spare. Many customers ask for 1.33 or more.

afterFigure.text: Cp compares widths and nothing else. It does not say where the process is centred, and a process can be as narrow as one likes and still be aimed at the wrong place, so Cp alone cannot say whether the parts are good. A second index is needed for that, and the next screens take it up.

steps.headline: Find Cp for limits of 49.90 and 50.10 mm and a standard deviation of 0.03 mm.

workedSteps.text: The tolerance range is the upper limit less the lower limit.
The spread of the process is 6 sigma.
Divide the tolerance range by the spread.

reveal.text: A tolerance that exactly equals the 6 sigma spread leaves no allowance for drift.

lead.text: Tool wear can move the mean of a process while leaving its spread unchanged.

reveal.text: Cp does not notice that the mean has moved. The next screen introduces an index that does.

steps.headline: Cpk measures the distance from the mean to the nearer limit, so it falls when the process drifts off centre.

lead.text: The index that accounts for centring is Cpk = (the distance from the mean to the nearer limit) / (3 sigma). With the mean at 25.02 mm and limits at 24.95 and 25.05 mm, the nearer limit is the upper one, 0.03 mm away, and Cpk = 0.03 / (3 x 0.01) = 1.0. A Cpk of 1.0 puts the nearer limit 3 sigma from the mean, so about 0.135 percent of parts are beyond it, even though Cp is still 1.67.

afterFigure.text: Cpk can never be larger than Cp, and the two are equal only when the mean sits exactly at the middle of the tolerance range. The figure keeps the spread fixed and moves the mean: at 25.00 mm Cpk is 1.67, at 25.02 mm it is 1.0, and at 25.04 mm it is 0.33, where about 16 percent of parts are above the upper limit. The remedy for a low Cpk with a high Cp is to recentre the process, which costs far less than narrowing it.

diagram.alt: Three bell curves with standard deviation 0.01 mm and limits at 24.95 and 25.05 mm. Centred on 25.00 mm, the process makes almost every part in limits and has a Cpk of 1.67. With its mean at 25.02 mm, a small tail passes the upper limit and Cpk is 1.0. With its mean at 25.04 mm, about 16 percent of parts are above the upper limit and Cpk is 0.33.
diagram.caption: The spread is the same in all three views, and only the mean moves. Cpk falls as the mean approaches a limit, while Cp stays at 1.67.

steps.headline: Find Cpk for a process with mean 24.985 mm and sigma 0.01 mm, with limits 24.95 and 25.05 mm.

workedSteps.text: The upper limit is 25.05 - 24.985 = 0.065 mm from the mean, and the lower limit is 24.985 - 24.95 = 0.035 mm away.
Cpk uses the nearer limit, divided by 3 sigma. Work it out to two decimal places.

reveal.text: Recentring recovers all of the capability that the spread allows, since Cpk rises to meet Cp.

steps.headline: Cpk says how few parts fall outside the limits, and measuring more parts does not change it.

lead.text: The share of parts beyond the nearer limit follows from Cpk, if the distribution is normal. At Cpk = 1.0 about 0.135 percent, or 1350 parts per million, lie beyond it. At 1.33 the figure is about 32 parts per million, and at 1.67 it is about 0.3. A centred process with Cp = 1.0 puts 0.27 percent beyond the two limits together, which is twice the single tail. The cards give these three values.

afterFigure.text: Two warnings apply. A high Cp does not guarantee good parts, as the drifted process showed. And measuring more parts does not improve a process: the capability is a property of the process, and a larger sample only gives a better estimate of it. To raise Cpk, the spread must be narrowed or the mean recentred, by better machines, better fixtures, better tools or tighter control.

diagram.alt: Three cards giving the share of parts beyond the nearer limit for a Cpk of 1.0, 1.33 and 1.67, from the normal distribution.
diagram.caption: The share of parts beyond the nearer limit falls very fast as Cpk rises. The values assume a normal distribution.

recap.keyIdea: Cp is the tolerance range divided by 6 sigma, Cpk uses the distance from the mean to the nearer limit divided by 3 sigma, and Cpk is never larger than Cp.

blocks.text: A process meets a tolerance when its spread fits inside it and its mean is near the middle. Cp, the tolerance range divided by 6 sigma, measures the fit, and Cpk, the nearer limit's distance from the mean divided by 3 sigma, also measures the centring, so a process with Cp = 1.67 and a mean at 25.02 mm has Cpk = 1.0, and about 0.135 percent of its parts are beyond the nearer limit.

lessons.title: Choosing a material and a process

reveal.text: A beam that is weaker in stiffness has to be made bulkier to compensate, and the next screens show by how much.

steps.headline: A material is chosen by working out what the part must do, and the performance index follows from the algebra.

lead.text: Selection begins with three questions. What must the part do, which is its **function**; what limits it, which are its **constraints**; and what should be as small as possible or as large as possible, which is its **objective**. Take a beam of a given length that must have a given stiffness S, with a mass that is to be as low as possible. The stiffness of a beam of square section with side b is proportional to E x b^4, so for a fixed S the side must be b proportional to 1 / E^(1/4). The mass is proportional to density x b^2, and putting in b gives a mass proportional to density / sqrt(E).

afterFigure.text: The lightest beam is therefore the one with the largest **performance index** sqrt(E) / density. This is not E alone, and not density alone: a stiffer material allows a smaller section, but only in proportion to the fourth root. The figure compares a steel beam with an aluminium one of the same stiffness, drawn to scale, and the aluminium has a larger section but a lower mass.

diagram.alt: Two square beam cross-sections drawn to scale, for beams of the same length and stiffness. The steel section has a side of 1.00 and the aluminium section a side of 1.32, which is 1.73 times the area, but aluminium is 0.34 times as dense, so the aluminium beam is lighter.
diagram.caption: To match a steel beam's stiffness, an aluminium beam must be larger, yet it still weighs less. The sizes are drawn to scale.

reveal.text: The index is a number for comparing, with no units that matter, since only its ranking is used.

steps.headline: Ranking by the performance index puts carbon-fibre composite and wood first, aluminium next and steel last.

lead.text: Calculating the index for common materials, with E in GPa and the density in g/cm3, gives steel 1.85, titanium 2.39, aluminium 3.10, pine 6.32 and a carbon-fibre composite 6.45. The mass of a beam with the same stiffness is proportional to the reciprocal of the index, so relative to steel an aluminium beam weighs 1.85 / 3.10 = 0.60, a titanium beam 0.77, and beams of pine or composite about 0.29. The aluminium beam saves 40 percent, not the 66 percent that its density alone suggests.

afterFigure.text: The charts show the ranking and its meaning in mass. Two details are worth noticing. The metals are close together, so choosing between them depends on other properties, while the composite and the wood are much better because they combine a high stiffness with a low density. And the ranking changes with the function: a tie rod in tension has the index E / density, and on that measure steel and aluminium are almost equal.

diagram.alt: Two bar charts for steel, titanium, aluminium, pine and carbon-fibre composite: the performance index square root of E over density, and the mass of an equal-stiffness beam relative to steel. Carbon-fibre composite and pine are best, aluminium next, and steel is worst.
diagram.caption: A high index means a light beam for a given stiffness. The mass chart is the same ranking turned into a weight.

steps.headline: The index ranks materials for one function, and cost, corrosion and the process can change the outcome.

lead.text: An index is a tool for one job, and the job has to be stated correctly. Different functions give different indices: a beam that must be stiff gives sqrt(E) / density, a tie rod gives E / density, and a beam that must be strong instead of stiff gives an index with the yield strength. Used on the wrong job, the ranking can be wrong. A second limit is that the index looks at one objective, and a real part also has a cost, a corrosion environment and a way of being made.

afterFigure.text: Aluminium rivets in a steel plate, an example from the corrosion lesson, would rank well on mass and fail in salt spray, because the galvanic cell makes the aluminium the anode. Cost may rule out carbon fibre, and wood suffers in wet conditions. The usual method is to rank by the index, then to screen the leading materials against these other limits, and to take the best that survives.

reveal.text: The best material depends on the job, and aluminium, a clear winner for a beam, gives no saving on a tie rod.

steps.headline: The process is chosen by the shape, the number of parts and the material, and it interacts with the choice of material.

lead.text: A process is chosen by what it can make. The **shape** rules some processes out: a hollow shape suits casting or moulding, a flat plate suits forming, a prismatic part with fine detail suits machining. The **volume** decides between processes with different tooling costs, as the break-even volume showed, so a few parts are printed or machined and thousands are cast or moulded. The **material** rules others out, because a thermoplastic is moulded and a carbon-fibre composite is **laid up**, built from layers of fibre sheet wetted with resin, and neither is cast.

afterFigure.text: Material and process therefore cannot be chosen separately. A beam in carbon-fibre composite needs a layup process and a certain shape, a die casting needs a metal that melts at a temperature the die can stand, and a high volume of small parts may force a change of material to suit a mould. The cards give the questions to ask, and the right answer comes from running through them for the actual job.

diagram.alt: Three cards matching a process to the job: by the shape, by the number of parts, and by the material.
diagram.caption: Shape, volume and material each rule some processes out. The choice is made by looking at all three.

cases.label: By shape

reveal.text: For one part the tooling cost dominates, and the process with no tooling wins.

lessons.orientation: Rank materials with a performance index and match process to shape, volume and material.
lessons.reviewLabel: Choosing a material and a process
lessons.nextAction: Choose a material and a process together for a real part, as this course has prepared you to do.

blocks.text: Aluminium is about a third as dense as steel, which makes it look like the obvious choice for a light beam, but it is also only a third as stiff. An aluminium beam made to bend no more than a steel one of the same length therefore needs a larger cross-section, and whether it still comes out lighter, and by how much, depends on how quickly the mass grows as the section is enlarged.

Questions of this kind are settled with a single number for each material, worked out from the algebra of what the part has to do, which ranks every material for that one job. Once the material is chosen, the process still has to suit the part's shape, the number wanted and the material itself, so the two choices end up being made together.

diagram.alt: Two square beam cross-sections drawn to scale, for beams of the same length and stiffness. The steel section has a side of 1.00 and the aluminium section a side of 1.32, which is 1.73 times the area, but aluminium is 0.34 times as dense, so the aluminium beam is lighter.
diagram.caption: To match a steel beam's stiffness, an aluminium beam must be larger, yet it still weighs less. The sizes are drawn to scale.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute a performance index, rank materials with it, and match a process to a part's shape, volume and material.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing the material and the process together is the last step from understanding materials to making things.

recap.keyIdea: A performance index, such as sqrt(E) / density for a stiff light beam, ranks materials for one job, and the process must be matched to the shape, the volume and the material.

blocks.text: For a beam of fixed stiffness the mass varies as density / sqrt(E), so materials are ranked by sqrt(E) / density: 1.85 for steel, 3.10 for aluminium, 6.45 for a carbon-fibre composite and 6.32 for pine, which makes an aluminium beam 0.60 of the mass of a steel one. The ranking holds for one function only, so cost, corrosion and the process have to be checked, and the process follows from shape, volume and material.

questions.prompt: A steel bar (E = 210 GPa) carries a stress of 105 MPa, within its elastic range. What is its strain, in percent?
hints: In the elastic range, strain is stress divided by the modulus E.
Convert E to MPa first: 210 GPa is 210,000 MPa.
Divide 105 by 210,000, then multiply by 100 to get a percent.
questions.onCorrect: Strain is 0.0005, so a 1 m length stretches by only 0.5 mm. Steel is stiff because E is large.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the strain as a plain ratio. The question asks for percent, so multiply by 100.
That divides 105 by 210 without converting GPa to MPa. 210 GPa is 210,000 MPa.

questions.prompt: The same steel yields at 250 MPa. It is pulled to 300 MPa and the load is then removed completely. What happens to the bar?
hints: Compare 300 MPa with the yield strength of 250 MPa.
Think about whether the stretch beyond yield is recovered.

acceptedIdeas: It stays slightly longer than before.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays slightly longer than before.

questions.onCorrect: Unloading follows a line parallel to the elastic one, so the plastic part of the stretch stays.

misconceptions.feedback: Steel is elastic only up to its yield strength. Beyond 250 MPa part of the stretch is permanent.
Removing load cannot break the bar. It follows a line parallel to the elastic one down to zero stress.

choices.label: It returns exactly to its original length, because steel is elastic.
It breaks as the load is removed.
It stays slightly longer than before.

questions.prompt: An alloy has E = 70 GPa. The 0.2 percent offset line has the elastic slope and starts at a strain of 0.002. At what strain, in percent, does that line reach 140 MPa?
hints: The offset line is the elastic line shifted along the strain axis.
Work out the strain the elastic line would have at 140 MPa, using E in MPa.
Add the offset of 0.002 to that strain, then convert to percent.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Elastic strain at 140 MPa is 140/70,000 = 0.002. Adding the offset 0.002 gives 0.004, which is 0.4 percent.

questions.onCorrect: The offset line sits 0.2 percent of strain to the right of the elastic line at every stress.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the elastic strain at 140 MPa, or the offset alone. The line reaches 140 MPa at the sum of the two.
That is the right strain as a ratio. The question asks for percent.

questions.prompt: The engineering stress falls after the peak of the curve while the bar is still being stretched. Why?
hints: Which area does engineering stress use?
What happens to the actual area of the bar in the neck?

acceptedIdeas: The load is divided by the original area, but the neck has a much smaller area.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The load is divided by the original area, but the neck has a much smaller area.

questions.onCorrect: True stress, which uses the neck's current area, keeps rising until fracture.

misconceptions.feedback: The metal in the neck is still strain hardening. The apparent weakening comes from how engineering stress is calculated.
The machine keeps pulling. The force on the bar falls because the neck cannot carry more load, while the stress calculation keeps the original area.

choices.label: The metal has started to weaken and can carry less stress.
The testing machine has begun to unload the bar.
The load is divided by the original area, but the neck has a much smaller area.

questions.prompt: Percent elongation divides the extension by which length: the original gauge length or the final length? Answer with one word, original or final.
hints: Strain is always measured against the bar before it was loaded.
questions.onCorrect: Dividing by the original gauge length makes elongation comparable between bars of any size.

misconceptions.feedback: Strain compares the stretch with the length the bar started with, since the final length already includes the stretch.

questions.prompt: The 10 mm bar fractures with a neck diameter of 8 mm. Using A0 = 78.54 mm2 and Af = 50.27 mm2, what is the reduction in area, in percent to one decimal place?
hints: Reduction in area is the lost area divided by the original area.
Subtract 50.27 from 78.54 first.
Divide that difference by 78.54 and multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The neck lost 36 percent of the original area, a plain sign of ductile behaviour.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final area as a share of the original. The reduction is what was lost.
That is the lost area in mm2. Divide it by the original area and express it as a percent.

questions.prompt: A bar carries an almost constant 300 MPa while it stretches to a fracture strain of 0.20. Treat the curve as a flat line at 300 MPa from zero strain. What is the toughness, in MJ/m3?
hints: Toughness is the area under the curve, here a rectangle.
A rectangle's area is height times width: stress times strain.
MPa multiplied by a strain ratio gives MJ per cubic metre directly.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The area is 300 MPa x 0.20 = 60 MPa, and 1 MPa is 1 MJ/m3, so the toughness is 60 MJ/m3.

questions.onCorrect: Because stress times strain is energy per volume, 1 MPa of stress over a strain of 1 equals 1 MJ/m3.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 25, as if the strain were a percent. Use 0.20 as a plain ratio.
That uses half the product, the area of a triangle. The curve here is flat, so the area is a rectangle.

questions.prompt: A tensile bar has a gauge length of 50 mm. At fracture the marks are 62 mm apart. What is the percent elongation?
hints: Find the extension first.
Divide the extension by the original gauge length, 50 mm.
Multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Elongation of 24 percent describes a ductile metal; glass would show a value close to zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the final length of 62 mm. Divide by the original gauge length.
That is the extension in millimetres. Divide it by 50 mm and express it as a percent.

questions.prompt: A 10 mm diameter bar fractures at a neck of 7 mm diameter. The areas are 78.54 mm2 and 38.48 mm2. What is the reduction in area, in percent to one decimal place?
hints: Subtract the final area from the original area.
Divide that difference by the original area.
Multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The area at the neck is less than half the original, so this metal deformed a great deal before it broke.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final area as a share of the original, 100 x 38.48 / 78.54. The reduction is what was lost.
That is the lost area in mm2. Divide by the original area to get a percent.

questions.prompt: What name is given to the slope of the straight, elastic part of a stress-strain curve?
hints: It is the ratio of stress to strain in the elastic region, and its symbol is E.
It is named for the English scientist Thomas Young.
questions.onCorrect: Young's modulus measures stiffness: how much stress is needed for a given elastic strain.

misconceptions.feedback: Yield strength is the stress where permanent deformation begins. The slope of the elastic line is a different quantity.
Toughness is the area under the whole curve, and it is not a slope.

questions.prompt: Neighbouring chains in a polymer such as polyethylene are held to each other by which kind of bond? Answer with its general name.
hints: The atoms along each chain are covalently bonded. The chains themselves attract each other more weakly.
These are the weakest of the four kinds of bond.
questions.onCorrect: Sliding chains past each other only has to overcome weak secondary bonds, which is why polymers soften when warmed.

misconceptions.feedback: Covalent bonds hold the atoms along each chain together. The attraction between chains is a different, weaker kind.
Polymer chains have no ions and no sea of electrons. The attraction between chains is the weakest of the four kinds.

questions.prompt: A ceramic's atoms are held by very strong ionic and covalent bonds. What do you expect its tensile curve to show?
hints: Think about the slope first: what do strong bonds do to E?
Then ask whether the atoms can slide past one another.

acceptedIdeas: A steep elastic line that ends in fracture with almost no plastic region.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A steep elastic line that ends in fracture with almost no plastic region.

questions.onCorrect: Ceramics are stiff and strong in compression, but their tensile curve ends where a flaw starts a crack.

misconceptions.feedback: Strong bonds give a high stiffness, but toughness needs plastic deformation, which these directional bonds resist.
Rigid, strong bonds give a steep elastic line, which means a high stiffness.

choices.label: A low stiffness, because the bonds hold the atoms rigidly in place.
A large plastic region, because strong bonds make a material tough.
A steep elastic line that ends in fracture with almost no plastic region.

questions.prompt: Nylon has E = 3 GPa and density 1.14 g/cm3. Find E divided by density, to one decimal place.
hints: Specific stiffness is E divided by density.
Divide 3 by 1.14.
Round to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 / 1.14 = 2.63, which is 2.6 to one decimal place.

questions.onCorrect: At 2.6, nylon has about a tenth of the stiffness per unit density of the metals.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies E by the density. Divide E by it.
That divides density by E. Put E on the top.

questions.prompt: To compare materials by stiffness per unit mass, E is divided by which other property?
hints: It is the property that gives mass for a given volume.
questions.onCorrect: Dividing by density asks how much stiffness each unit of mass buys.

questions.prompt: Titanium has E = 116 GPa and density 4.5 g/cm3. Find E divided by density, to one decimal place.
hints: Divide E by the density.
116 / 4.5 is a little under 26.
Round 25.78 to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: Titanium lands within a few percent of steel and aluminium on this measure.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies E by the density. Divide E by it.

questions.prompt: A glass-fibre composite has E = 40 GPa and density 1.9 g/cm3. Find E divided by density, to one decimal place.
hints: Divide E by the density.
40 / 1.9 is a little over 21.
Round to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 / 1.9 = 21.05, which is 21.1 to one decimal place.

questions.onCorrect: A plastic made of glass fibres reaches about 80 percent of the metals' value, so plastics are not weak by nature.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies E by the density. Divide E by it.
That is the value for nylon, a plastic without fibres.

questions.prompt: Aluminium has E = 70 GPa and density 2.70 g/cm3. Find E divided by density, to one decimal place.
hints: Divide E by the density.
70 / 2.7 is close to 26.
Round 25.93 to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: Steel gives 26.8, so aluminium's stiffness per unit density is almost the same as steel's.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies E by the density. Divide E by it.

questions.prompt: In a copper wire, the outer electrons are shared among all the atoms. What kind of bond is this?
hints: The positive ions sit in a sea of electrons that belong to the whole piece.
questions.onCorrect: Because the sea of electrons is not tied to any pair of atoms, layers of copper can slide, which makes copper ductile.

misconceptions.feedback: Covalent bonds share electrons between a particular pair of atoms. In a metal the electrons belong to all the atoms.
Ionic bonds link positive and negative ions. A copper wire has only one kind of atom.

questions.prompt: Which family is hard and very stiff, strong in compression, brittle in tension, and held together by ionic and covalent bonds?
hints: Think of window glass and brick.
questions.onCorrect: Ceramics owe their hardness to bonds that resist both stretching and sliding.

misconceptions.feedback: Metals are held by metallic bonds and are ductile, which lets them yield instead of breaking suddenly.
Polymers have low stiffness because weak secondary bonds hold their chains together.
Composites combine two materials, and their properties come from that combination instead of one kind of bond.

choices.label: Ceramics and glasses
Polymers
Metals
Composites

questions.prompt: Plastic deformation in a metal happens by the movement of a line defect in the crystal. What is this defect called?
hints: The figure showed an extra half plane of atoms ending inside the crystal.
The word begins with dis-, as in displaced.
questions.onCorrect: Only the bonds along the dislocation line are stretched at any moment, so far less stress is needed than to slide a whole plane.

misconceptions.feedback: A vacancy is a missing atom, and it is a point defect. The defect that carries plastic flow is a line of misfit.

questions.prompt: Two samples of the same metal differ only in grain size: one has coarse grains and the other fine grains. Which one is stronger?
hints: Think about what a grain boundary does to a moving dislocation.
More boundaries per millimetre means more obstacles.
questions.onCorrect: Each boundary is an obstacle, and a fine-grained metal has many more of them in any line across it.

misconceptions.feedback: Bigger grains give dislocations a longer run before they meet a boundary, so a coarse metal yields more easily.
The bonds are the same, but strength depends on how easily dislocations move, and boundaries slow them.

choices.label: The fine-grained sample.
The coarse-grained sample, because its grains are bigger.
They are the same, because the bonds are the same.

questions.prompt: Using strength = 50 + 20 / square root of d, with d in mm and strength in MPa, find the yield strength for a grain size of 0.04 mm.
hints: Take the square root of 0.04 first.
Divide 20 by that square root.
Add the 50 MPa.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The square root of 0.04 is 0.2, so 20 / 0.2 = 100, and 50 + 100 = 150 MPa.

questions.onCorrect: A grain size of 0.04 mm lies between the two in the figure, so its strength falls between their 100 and 300 MPa.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 20 x 0.04 = 0.8 to 50. The grain size appears as 1 over its square root.
That is only the grain term. The constant 50 MPa has to be added to it.

questions.prompt: Now use d = 0.0025 mm. The square root of d is 0.05. What is the yield strength, in MPa?
hints: Divide 20 by 0.05.
Add 50 MPa to the result.
Check that the answer is bigger than 250 MPa, since the grains are finer.
questions.onCorrect: Cutting the grain size by a factor of four doubles the grain term, because the square root of 4 is 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the grain term. Add the constant 50 MPa.
That multiplies 20 by 0.0025 instead of dividing by the square root of d.

questions.prompt: Heating a cold-worked metal so that new, strain-free grains form and the metal softens again is called what?
hints: The same word is used for softening glass and steel by heating and slow cooling.
questions.onCorrect: Annealing removes the tangled dislocations by letting new strain-free grains grow, which restores ductility.

misconceptions.feedback: Quenching is fast cooling, and in steel it hardens the metal. The softening treatment is a slow heating and cooling.

questions.prompt: A metal follows strength = 50 + 20 / square root of d, with d in mm. What grain size gives a yield strength of 350 MPa? Give d in mm to four decimal places.
hints: Subtract the constant 50 from 350 first.
Divide 20 by that result to get the square root of d.
Square it.
questions.onCorrect: The answer is about 4.4 micrometres, between the 0.01 mm and 0.0025 mm grain sizes already met.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the square root of d. Square it to get d.
That divides 20 by 350 without removing the constant 50 MPa first.

questions.prompt: Using strength = 50 + 20 / square root of d, with d in mm, what is the yield strength for d = 0.0016 mm?
hints: The square root of 0.0016 is 0.04.
Divide 20 by 0.04.
Add 50 MPa.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The square root of 0.0016 is 0.04, so 20 / 0.04 = 500, and 50 + 500 = 550 MPa.

questions.onCorrect: A grain of 1.6 micrometres is very fine, and the formula gives more than twice the strength of the 0.01 mm sample.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the grain term. Add the 50 MPa constant.
That multiplies 20 by d. The grain size appears as one over its square root.

questions.prompt: Real metals yield at a small fraction of the stress needed to slide one whole plane of a perfect crystal over another. Why?
hints: Recall what the extra half plane does when it moves.
Compare breaking all the bonds at once with breaking them one row at a time.

acceptedIdeas: Slip moves a dislocation, so only a few bonds are stretched at a time.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Slip moves a dislocation, so only a few bonds are stretched at a time.

questions.onCorrect: The rug picture fits: a ripple moves along a rug and shifts it a little with each step, without dragging the whole rug at once.

misconceptions.feedback: The bonds are the same. What differs is that slip happens by movement of a defect instead of a whole plane.
Whole planes do not slide at once in a real metal. A dislocation carries the slip one row at a time.

choices.label: The bonds in real metals are much weaker than in a perfect crystal.
Whole planes slide, but each plane is thinner than in a perfect crystal.
Slip moves a dislocation, so only a few bonds are stretched at a time.

questions.prompt: Drawing a copper wire through dies makes it harder and more brittle by multiplying and tangling its dislocations. What is this strengthening process called?
hints: The metal is deformed at room temperature, which is why it is sometimes called cold working.
The name says that doing work on the metal hardens it.
questions.onCorrect: Work hardening raises strength and lowers ductility, and annealing reverses it.

misconceptions.feedback: Annealing is the treatment that softens the metal again. The process that hardened it is the opposite one.

questions.prompt: For d = 0.01 mm, what is the boundary term 20 / square root of d, in MPa?
hints: The square root of 0.01 is 0.1.
Divide 20 by that square root.
The answer is a whole number of tens.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The square root of 0.01 is 0.1, and 20 / 0.1 = 200 MPa.

questions.onCorrect: This is the part of the strength that the boundaries add, and it is four times the constant 50 MPa.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 20 by 0.1. The square root is in the denominator.

questions.prompt: On slow cooling through 727 C, austenite with 0.76 percent carbon becomes a structure of alternating thin layers of ferrite and cementite. What is it called?
hints: It is named for the mother-of-pearl sheen of its layers under a microscope.
The word appears in the diagram's labels.
questions.onCorrect: Pearlite is about nine tenths ferrite by mass, so it combines ferrite's ductility with a hard cementite skeleton.

misconceptions.feedback: Martensite forms only when the steel is cooled too fast for carbon to move. Slow cooling gives layers of ferrite and cementite.

questions.prompt: Two steels are cooled slowly. One has 0.2 percent carbon and the other 0.8 percent. How do their strengths compare?
hints: Cementite is hard. Which steel has more of it?

acceptedIdeas: The 0.8 percent steel is much stronger, and less ductile.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 0.8 percent steel is much stronger, and less ductile.

questions.onCorrect: Each extra tenth of a percent of carbon adds hard cementite, so strength rises and ductility falls.

misconceptions.feedback: Carbon content and heat treatment can change the strength of steel severalfold, so steel is a family of materials.
More carbon gives more cementite, and the extra cementite raises strength.

choices.label: The 0.2 percent steel is stronger, because it has less brittle cementite.
They are about equal, because both are steel.
The 0.8 percent steel is much stronger, and less ductile.

questions.prompt: The lever rule gives the share of a phase from the arm of the bar on which side: the arm near that phase's end, or the far arm? Answer near or far.
hints: Think of a see-saw: a heavy load close to the pivot needs only a short arm to balance.
questions.onCorrect: A steel close to the pearlite end has mostly pearlite, and its far arm, the one reaching to ferrite, is the long one.

misconceptions.feedback: The near arm gives the share of the other phase. Check with a steel at 0.76 percent carbon: it is all pearlite, and its near arm has length zero.

questions.prompt: A steel contains 0.60 percent carbon and is cooled slowly to just below 727 C. The ferrite end of the bar is at 0.022 and the pearlite end at 0.76. What fraction of the steel is pearlite, to three decimal places?
hints: The arm on the ferrite side is 0.60 - 0.022.
The whole bar is 0.76 - 0.022.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: A steel with 0.60 percent carbon is about 78 percent pearlite and 22 percent proeutectoid ferrite.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction of ferrite. Pearlite uses the arm on the ferrite side.
That divides by 0.76 and not by the whole bar of 0.738.

questions.prompt: If austenite is cooled so fast that carbon cannot move out of the iron lattice, a very hard, brittle structure forms. What is it called?
hints: It is named for the German metallurgist Adolf Martens.
It is not pearlite, and it forms only on fast cooling.
questions.onCorrect: Martensite is iron with carbon trapped in a strained lattice, which blocks dislocations very effectively.

misconceptions.feedback: Pearlite forms on slow cooling, when carbon has time to move into layers of cementite.

questions.prompt: A steel cooled slowly is to contain 50 percent pearlite, as the lever rule gives it just below 727 C. What carbon content gives this, in weight percent to two decimal places?
hints: Write the fraction as (C - 0.022) / 0.738 and set it to 0.50.
Multiply 0.50 by 0.738.
questions.onCorrect: About 0.39 percent carbon, which is near the middle of the bar between 0.022 and 0.76.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the 0.022 at the ferrite end, which has to be added back.
That is the midpoint of 0 and 0.76. The bar starts at 0.022, not 0.

questions.prompt: A 0.30 percent carbon steel is cooled slowly to just below 727 C. What fraction of it is pearlite, to three decimal places?
hints: The arm on the ferrite side is 0.30 - 0.022.
The whole bar is 0.738 long.
Divide the arm by the whole bar.
questions.onCorrect: Roughly 38 percent pearlite, with the other 62 percent as soft proeutectoid ferrite.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction of ferrite. Pearlite uses the arm on the ferrite side.
That divides by 0.76 and not by 0.738.

questions.prompt: The reheating of a quenched steel to a temperature below 727 C, to trade some hardness for toughness, is called what?
hints: The word is also used for chocolate and for moods that are kept in check.
It follows quenching in the usual treatment.
questions.onCorrect: Tempering lets some of the trapped carbon leave the martensite as carbides, which relieves brittleness.

misconceptions.feedback: Annealing is a slow heating and cooling that makes steel soft. The reheating that follows a quench is a gentler treatment.

questions.prompt: A chef's knife is quenched and must stay very hard at the edge, with only some of the brittleness removed. Which treatment fits?
hints: Which tempering temperature keeps the hardness closer to the as-quenched value?
questions.onCorrect: At 200 C the hardness stays close to its quenched value and a little of the brittleness goes.

misconceptions.feedback: Tempering at 500 C gives a tough but noticeably softer steel, which would not hold a sharp edge.
Steel as quenched is hard but brittle, and a knife in that state would chip.
Annealing makes steel soft and would undo the hardening.

choices.label: Temper it at 500 C
Anneal it
Temper it at 200 C
Leave it as quenched

questions.prompt: A cured epoxy cannot be melted again, because its chains are linked together by covalent cross-links. What class of polymer is this?
hints: The class is named for the way heat sets it permanently.
questions.onCorrect: Cross-links tie the chains into a single network, so heating cannot let them slide past each other and the polymer cannot flow.

misconceptions.feedback: A thermoplastic has no cross-links, so heating lets its chains slide and the polymer melts. Epoxy does not melt.

questions.prompt: A rubber band has a glass transition temperature of about -70 C. At room temperature, is it above or below its glass transition? Answer above or below.
hints: Room temperature is around 20 C, and -70 C is far colder.
questions.onCorrect: Above Tg the chains can move, so the rubber band is soft and stretchy. Cooled well below -70 C it would turn glassy and could shatter.

misconceptions.feedback: Room temperature of about 20 C is warmer than -70 C, so the rubber is warmer than its glass transition.

questions.prompt: A bar of a ceramic is tested twice, once pulled in tension and once squeezed in compression. How do the failure stresses compare?
hints: Think about what each load does to a small flaw in the surface.

acceptedIdeas: Compression is much higher than tension.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compression is much higher than tension.

questions.onCorrect: Ceramics are often used in compression, such as bricks and concrete, for this reason.

misconceptions.feedback: A flaw in a ceramic opens under tension, so the failure stress is low there. A metal would yield first instead.
The bonds are the same, but a flaw behaves differently: tension opens it and compression closes it.

choices.label: Compression is much higher than tension.
They are about the same, because the bonds are the same.
Tension is much higher than compression, as for most metals.

questions.prompt: Along the fibres, fibre and matrix are stretched together. Do they share the same strain or the same stress? Answer strain or stress.
hints: They are bonded together and stretch by the same amount.
questions.onCorrect: Equal strain means the stress in each part is its modulus times that strain, so the stiffer fibre carries most of the load.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal stress is the case across the fibres. Along them, bonded parts must stretch by the same amount.

questions.prompt: For the same composite, with Ef = 230 GPa, Em = 3 GPa and 60 percent fibre, the stiffness across the fibres follows 1 / E = 0.6 / 230 + 0.4 / 3. What is E, in GPa to two decimal places?
hints: Work out each term: 0.6 / 230 and 0.4 / 3.
Add the two and take the reciprocal.
The answer is only a little more than twice the matrix stiffness.
questions.onCorrect: Across the fibres the soft matrix dominates, so the composite is only about 2.5 times as stiff as the epoxy, and 19 times less stiff than along the fibres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stiffness along the fibres, where the stiffnesses add by volume. Across them, the compliances add.
That averages the two stiffnesses without weighting them by volume.

questions.prompt: A glass-fibre composite has fibres with Ef = 70 GPa and a matrix with Em = 3 GPa, and 50 percent fibre by volume. What is its stiffness along the fibres, in GPa?
hints: Along the fibres the stiffnesses add in proportion to volume.
Multiply each stiffness by its volume fraction.
Add the two products.
questions.onCorrect: The fibres supply 35 of the 36.5 GPa, since they are far stiffer than the matrix.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stiffness across the fibres. Along them, add the stiffnesses weighted by volume.
That adds the two stiffnesses and leaves out the volume fractions.

questions.prompt: For the same glass-fibre composite, with Ef = 70 GPa, Em = 3 GPa and 50 percent fibre, find the stiffness across the fibres, in GPa to two decimal places.
hints: Across the fibres the compliances, 1 / E, add in proportion to volume.
Take the reciprocal.
questions.onCorrect: Across the fibres the composite is more than six times less stiff than along them, which is why layers of fibre are laid in several directions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stiffness along the fibres. Across them, add the compliances, 1 / E.
That is 1 / E. Take its reciprocal to get E.

questions.prompt: A carbon-fibre composite has Ef = 230 GPa, Em = 3 GPa and 40 percent fibre. What is its stiffness along the fibres, in GPa?
hints: Along the fibres the stiffnesses add in proportion to volume.
The matrix fraction is 0.6.
Add 0.4 x 230 and 0.6 x 3.
questions.onCorrect: Reducing the fibre fraction from 60 to 40 percent lowers the stiffness along the fibres from 139.2 to 93.8 GPa.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the across-fibre value. Along the fibres, add stiffnesses weighted by volume.
That averages the two stiffnesses without weighting them by volume.

questions.prompt: A polyethylene shopping bag can be melted and remoulded into a new shape. What class of polymer is it?
hints: Its chains are not cross-linked, so heating lets them slide.
questions.onCorrect: Because the chains are held only by weak secondary bonds, warming lets them flow, and cooling sets them again.

misconceptions.feedback: Thermosets are cross-linked and cannot be melted. A shopping bag can, so it is the other class.

questions.prompt: Window glass fails from tiny surface flaws when it is loaded in one way, yet thick glass blocks bear large loads in the other. Which kind of loading do ceramics resist far better, tension or compression?
hints: Which load closes a crack instead of opening it?
questions.onCorrect: In compression the flaws close and cannot grow, so the strength is governed by the bonds and not by the flaws.

misconceptions.feedback: Tension opens surface flaws and lets cracks grow, so a ceramic is weakest there.

questions.prompt: A plate carries a stress of 100 MPa and has a crack of length a = 1 mm. Take Y = 1. Find K = Y x stress x square root of (pi x a), with a in metres, in MPa times the square root of metres.
hints: Convert 1 mm to metres first.
Work out pi x 0.001, then its square root.
Multiply by 100 MPa.
questions.onCorrect: At 5.6 this is far below the toughness of steel, about 50, so the crack does not grow.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses a in millimetres. The formula needs the crack length in metres.
That leaves out the stress of 100 MPa as a multiplier.

questions.prompt: A crack in a steel part grows to twice its length, while the part and the material stay the same. Roughly how does the stress at which the crack will run change?
hints: The stress intensity grows with the square root of the crack length.
Doubling the length multiplies its square root by about 1.41.

acceptedIdeas: It falls, but only to about 0.7 of what it was.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls, but only to about 0.7 of what it was.

questions.onCorrect: Halving the critical stress needs a crack four times as long, because of the square root.

misconceptions.feedback: The toughness of the material is the same, but a longer crack concentrates the stress more, so a lower applied stress is enough to make it run.
Halving would follow if the stress went as 1 over the crack length, but the stress intensity grows with the square root of the length, so the stress falls by 1 / sqrt(2), about 0.71.
A longer crack concentrates more stress at its tip, so it runs at a lower applied stress.

choices.label: It falls, but only to about 0.7 of what it was.
It stays the same, because the material is the same.
It rises, because a longer crack spreads the load.
It falls to about half.

questions.prompt: The crack in the worked example is 2 mm long. What is its length in metres?
hints: There are 1000 mm in a metre.
Divide the length in millimetres by 1000.
The answer is a few thousandths of a metre.
questions.onCorrect: The units of K, MPa times square root of metres, need the crack length in metres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length in millimetres. The formula needs metres.

questions.prompt: A steel with K_IC = 50 MPa sqrt(m) carries 200 MPa, with Y = 1. The critical crack length is a = (K_IC / stress)^2 / pi. What is a in mm, to one decimal place?
hints: Divide 50 by 200 and square the result.
Divide by pi, giving a in metres.
Multiply by 1000 to get millimetres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (50 / 200)^2 = 0.0625, divided by pi is 0.01989 m, which is 19.9 mm.

questions.onCorrect: At 200 MPa the steel tolerates a crack of nearly 20 mm, where at 400 MPa the limit is about 5 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a in metres. Multiply by 1000 for millimetres.
That leaves out dividing by pi.

questions.prompt: Many steels are tough when warm and absorb little energy when cold, with the change over a narrow range of temperature. What is this change called?
hints: It is named for the two kinds of failure the steel changes between.
questions.onCorrect: Below the transition the steel fractures without yielding first, so a crack runs with little warning.

misconceptions.feedback: The glass transition belongs to polymers, where chains stop moving. A steel's change is in how it fractures.

questions.prompt: A high-strength steel has K_IC = 30 MPa sqrt(m) and works at 600 MPa. What is its critical crack length, in mm to one decimal place?
hints: Divide 30 by 600 and square it.
Divide by pi to get metres.
Convert to millimetres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (30 / 600)^2 = 0.0025, divided by pi is 0.000796 m, which is 0.8 mm.

questions.onCorrect: The stronger steel tolerates a crack of 0.8 mm, against 5.0 mm for a tougher one at 400 MPa, so strength alone does not make a part safer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a in metres. Multiply by 1000 for millimetres.
That leaves out dividing by pi.

questions.prompt: A steel has K_IC = 60 MPa sqrt(m), Y = 1 and a crack of length 1 mm. What stress makes the crack grow, in MPa to the nearest 10?
hints: Convert 1 mm to metres, 0.001 m.
Compute the square root of pi x 0.001.
Divide 60 by it.
questions.onCorrect: Even a 1 mm crack lets the steel carry more than 1000 MPa, but the margin falls quickly as the crack grows.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the square root of pi times a. The critical stress divides K_IC by it.
That uses a in millimetres. The formula needs metres.

questions.prompt: A steel has K_IC = 50 MPa sqrt(m) and carries 400 MPa, with Y = 1. What is the critical crack length, in mm to one decimal place?
hints: Divide 50 by 400 and square the result.
Divide by pi.
Convert metres to millimetres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (50 / 400)^2 = 0.015625, divided by pi is 0.004974 m, which is 5.0 mm.

questions.onCorrect: At 400 MPa the steel tolerates a crack about 5 mm long, so inspection must find cracks well below that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a in metres. Multiply by 1000 for millimetres.
That leaves out dividing by pi.

questions.prompt: A welded structure in the same steel is to work in cold sea water. Which change makes a crack in it more dangerous?
hints: Think about the steel's energy absorbed against temperature.

acceptedIdeas: A lower temperature, if the steel has a ductile-brittle transition.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A lower temperature, if the steel has a ductile-brittle transition.

questions.onCorrect: Brittle fractures in welded ships in cold seas in the 1940s were of this kind.

misconceptions.feedback: Paint protects the surface from corrosion but does not change how the steel fractures.
A higher yield strength with the same K_IC changes the stress at which the steel yields, but not the stress at which a crack runs.
A lower load reduces the stress at the crack tip, so it makes a crack safer.

choices.label: A lower load on the structure.
A higher yield strength with the same toughness.
A lower temperature, if the steel has a ductile-brittle transition.
A thicker coat of paint.

questions.prompt: In the corrosion cell on a wet steel surface, iron dissolves into the water at one site. What is the site where the metal dissolves called?
hints: Oxidation takes place there, and electrons are released.
questions.onCorrect: The anode is where the metal gives up electrons and goes into solution, so it is the part that is lost.

misconceptions.feedback: At the cathode oxygen takes up electrons and no metal is lost. The metal dissolves at the other site.

questions.prompt: Aluminium rivets hold together two large steel plates, and the joint is sprayed with salt water. Which metal corrodes first?
hints: Compare the electrode potentials of aluminium and iron.
The more negative potential is the anode.
questions.onCorrect: The aluminium is the anode and the large steel plates are the cathode, which makes the small rivets lose metal quickly.

misconceptions.feedback: In a joint the more active metal is the anode. Aluminium is more active than iron, so it is the aluminium that is lost.
Joining different metals in an electrolyte makes a galvanic cell, which makes corrosion faster for the more active metal.

choices.label: The aluminium rivets.
The steel plates, because iron rusts.
Neither, because the metals are different.

questions.prompt: How many electrons does each iron atom release when it dissolves as an Fe2+ ion?
hints: Look at the charge written beside the ion.
Each unit of positive charge on an ion means one electron has been lost.
Read the number in the superscript.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Fe goes to Fe2+, which means the atom loses two electrons.

questions.onCorrect: In the formula for metal loss this number is called n.

misconceptions.feedback: The ion carries more than one unit of positive charge, and each unit stands for one electron lost.

questions.prompt: A zinc sacrificial anode (M = 65.38 g/mol, n = 2) supplies a current of 0.02 A for one year, 3.156 x 10^7 s. Using m = I x t x M / (n x F), with F = 96485 C/mol, how many grams of zinc are lost?
hints: Charge passed is I x t: 0.02 x 3.156e7 coulombs.
Multiply by M and divide by n x F.
The result is a little over 200 g.
questions.onCorrect: A 2 kg zinc anode with this current would last about nine years.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out dividing by n = 2.

questions.prompt: A block of zinc is bolted to a steel ship's hull and corrodes in place of the steel. What is such a block called?
hints: It is sacrificed so that the hull is not.
questions.onCorrect: The zinc is more active than steel, so it becomes the anode of a cell, and the steel hull becomes the cathode.

misconceptions.feedback: The block corrodes, so it is the anode of the cell. The hull is the one that is protected.

questions.prompt: A steel part corrodes at a steady 0.01 A. How long will it take to lose 10 g of iron (M = 55.85 g/mol, n = 2), in days to the nearest day?
hints: Rearrange m = I x t x M / (n x F) to make t the subject.
t = m x n x F / (I x M), in seconds.
Divide the seconds by 86,400 to get days.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: t = m x n x F / (I x M) = 10 x 2 x 96485 / (0.01 x 55.85) = 3.455e6 s, which is 40 days.

questions.onCorrect: A corrosion current of only 10 mA removes 10 g of iron in about six weeks.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. Divide by 86,400 for days.
That divides in the wrong order. The mass is on the top of the fraction.

questions.prompt: A current of 2 A dissolves aluminium (M = 26.98 g/mol, n = 3) for one hour, 3600 s. Using m = I x t x M / (n x F) with F = 96485 C/mol, how many grams of aluminium are lost? Give the answer to two decimal places.
hints: Charge is I x t: 2 x 3600 coulombs.
Multiply by M and divide by n x F.
n is 3 for Al3+.
questions.onCorrect: Aluminium gives three electrons per atom and is light, so a given current takes about a third of a gram per ampere hour.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out dividing by n = 3.
That is the answer in moles of electrons divided by n. Multiply by the molar mass.

questions.prompt: A copper pipe is joined to a steel pipe in wet conditions. Which metal corrodes?
hints: Compare the electrode potentials of iron and copper.

acceptedIdeas: The steel, because it is more active than copper.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The steel, because it is more active than copper.

questions.onCorrect: The steel is the anode of the galvanic cell, and copper is the cathode, which loses no metal.

misconceptions.feedback: Value has nothing to do with it. The more active metal is the anode, and copper is the less active of the two.
Copper is noble, but the contact makes the steel the anode of a cell, so the steel corrodes faster.
One metal is the anode and the other the cathode, so only the anode loses metal.

choices.label: The steel, because it is more active than copper.
Neither, because copper is noble and protects the steel.
Both corrode at the same rate.
The copper, because copper is the more valuable metal.

questions.prompt: Coating steel with a layer of zinc, so that the zinc corrodes first even where the coating is scratched, is called what? Use the British or American spelling.
hints: The name honours Luigi Galvani, who studied the effects of electricity on animal tissue.
questions.onCorrect: The zinc coating works because zinc is the more active metal, so it is the anode even in the scratch.

misconceptions.feedback: Paint is only a barrier, and a scratch lets the steel rust beneath it. The coating that protects a scratch is a metal.

questions.prompt: A block 200 mm by 100 mm by 50 mm has volume 1,000,000 mm3 and surface area 70,000 mm2. What is V / A, in mm to one decimal place?
hints: Divide the volume by the surface area.
Both are in millimetre units, so the result is in mm.
questions.onCorrect: V / A is a length that measures how thick the casting is, in the sense that matters for freezing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the area in cm2. Divide the volume by the area.
That is V / A in cm. The question asks for mm.

questions.prompt: A cube of side 200 mm is cast in the same mould material as a cube of side 100 mm, so its ratio of volume to surface area, V / A, is twice as large. Roughly how much longer does the larger cube take to freeze?
hints: Heat leaves through the surface, so compare how much metal lies behind each square millimetre of surface.
The larger cube has eight times the volume and four times the surface area.
