questions.onCorrect: Freezing time goes with the square of V / A, so doubling the ratio gives four times the time, even though the larger cube holds eight times the metal.

misconceptions.feedback: The mould is the same, but the larger cube has twice as much metal behind each square millimetre of surface, so it takes longer to lose its heat.
The time grows faster than V / A, because Chvorinov's rule makes it depend on the square of V / A, so twice the ratio gives four times the time.
The larger cube holds eight times the metal, but it also has four times the surface to lose heat through, so its freezing time grows by less than eight.

choices.label: About the same time, because the mould is the same.
About four times as long.
About eight times as long, in step with the volume.
About twice as long, in step with V / A.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, V / A is 1.667 cm. What is 1.667 squared?
hints: Multiply 1.667 by itself.
1.667 x 1.667 is a little under 2.8.
Round to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: The square, 2.78 cm2, is multiplied by B in the next step.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles 1.667 instead of squaring it.

questions.prompt: Now cast a cube of side 50 mm, with the same B = 2 min/cm2. V / A is 0.8333 cm. What is the freezing time, in minutes to two decimal places?
hints: Square 0.8333.
Multiply the result by B = 2.
The time is about a quarter of the 5.56 minutes of the larger cube.
questions.onCorrect: The small cube freezes in 1.39 minutes, a quarter of the 5.56 minutes for the cube of 100 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies V / A by 2 without squaring it first.
That leaves out the mould constant B = 2.

questions.prompt: A casting is to be 490 mm long after it has cooled, and the metal shrinks 2 percent in length as it cools. How long, in mm, must the pattern be? The pattern is larger by the factor 1 / (1 - 0.02).
hints: The casting is 98 percent of the pattern.
Divide the casting length by 0.98.
Do not add 2 percent to 490.
questions.onCorrect: The pattern is 500 mm, and 2 percent of 500 mm is 10 mm, which is the shrinkage in the casting.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 percent of 490 to the casting length. The 2 percent is of the pattern, not the casting.
That subtracts the allowance. The pattern must be larger than the casting.

questions.prompt: One large casting is needed, once, for a prototype that will be machined afterwards. Which casting process fits best?
hints: The tooling cost must stay low for a single part.

acceptedIdeas: Sand casting, because its pattern is cheap.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sand casting, because its pattern is cheap.

questions.onCorrect: Sand casting uses a cheap, expendable mould, so the cost per part is high but the cost of starting is low.

misconceptions.feedback: Die casting needs a steel mould that costs a great deal, and that pays back only over thousands of parts.
For a single part the tooling is the whole difference, since a die costs a great deal and a sand pattern very little.

choices.label: Die casting, because its parts come out accurate and cheap.
Either, because for a single part the tooling cost makes no difference.
Sand casting, because its pattern is cheap.

questions.prompt: A casting section has V / A = 1.2 cm. A riser has V / A = 1.5 cm, and the mould constant B is the same for both. How many times longer does the riser take to freeze, to two decimal places?
hints: The mould constant cancels in the ratio.
Divide 1.5 by 1.2 and square the result.
Compare with 1.25 squared.
questions.onCorrect: The riser freezes about 1.6 times as long as the casting, which leaves time for it to feed liquid metal.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio of V / A. The times go as the square of it.
That divides the casting by the riser. Divide the riser's time by the casting's.

questions.prompt: Two casting sections of the same metal have V / A of 20 mm and 30 mm. How many times longer does the second take to freeze, to two decimal places?
hints: Divide 30 by 20.
Freezing time goes as V / A squared.
Square the ratio.
questions.onCorrect: A section 1.5 times thicker takes more than twice as long, which is the reason a casting should have even thickness.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio of V / A. Square it.
That cubes the ratio. The time depends on its square.

questions.prompt: A casting must measure 588 mm after cooling, and the metal shrinks 2 percent. How long, in mm, must the pattern be?
hints: The casting is 98 percent of the pattern.
Divide the casting length by 0.98.
Check by taking 2 percent of your answer: it should equal the shrinkage.
questions.onCorrect: The pattern is 600 mm, so the 12 mm of shrinkage brings the casting to 588 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 percent of 588. The 2 percent is of the pattern, not the casting.
That subtracts the allowance. The pattern must be larger.

questions.prompt: Why must a riser be shaped so that it freezes after the casting it feeds?
hints: Think about where the shrinkage cavity ends up.

acceptedIdeas: So that it can supply liquid metal to the casting while the casting shrinks.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: So that it can supply liquid metal to the casting while the casting shrinks.

questions.onCorrect: A riser that freezes last takes the shrinkage hole into itself, and the sound casting is separated from it afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: A riser that is too small freezes first and cannot feed the casting. It has to be bigger in V / A than the section it feeds.
If both froze together, the casting would have no liquid metal to make up its shrinkage.
Cutting it off is a later step, and it has no effect on whether the casting is sound.

choices.label: So that the casting freezes at the same time as the riser.
So that the riser is as small as possible.
So that it can supply liquid metal to the casting while the casting shrinks.
So that the riser can be cut off more easily.

questions.prompt: A billet 50 mm tall with a cross-section of 2000 mm2 is forged down to 20 mm tall. Assuming the volume stays the same, what is the new cross-sectional area, in mm2?
hints: Work out the volume first: height times area.
The volume does not change during forging.
Divide the volume by the new height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The volume is 50 x 2000 = 100,000 mm3, so the new area is 100,000 / 20 = 5000 mm2.

questions.onCorrect: Squeezing metal does not compress it. It makes the billet wider, so the area grows as the height falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales by height ratio the wrong way round. The shorter billet must be wider, not narrower. Divide the volume by 20 mm.
That keeps the area unchanged. The volume is constant, so a shorter billet has a larger area.

questions.prompt: A plate is rolled 25 percent thinner, and then rolled another 25 percent thinner than it is at that point. Roughly what is the total reduction in thickness?
hints: The second 25 percent is a fraction of the thickness after the first pass.
Is 25 percent of a thinner plate more or less than 25 percent of the original?
questions.onCorrect: The total is 43.75 percent, since 0.75 x 0.75 = 0.5625 of the thickness remains, and percentages of different thicknesses do not add.

misconceptions.feedback: The second 25 percent is taken from a plate that is already thinner, so it removes less than the first did and the total falls short of 50 percent.
Work hardening changes the force needed, but the rolls set the reduction, and the second 25 percent comes off a thinner plate, so the total is below 50 percent.

choices.label: A little more than 50 percent, because the second pass works on harder metal.
Exactly 50 percent, because 25 and 25 make 50.
A little less than 50 percent.

questions.prompt: True strain in rolling is the natural logarithm of a ratio of the starting and final thicknesses. Does the starting thickness sit on the top or the bottom of that fraction? Answer top or bottom.
hints: The fraction is greater than 1 when the plate gets thinner.
questions.onCorrect: Putting the larger starting thickness on top gives a positive strain for a reduction in thickness.

misconceptions.feedback: With the starting thickness on the bottom the fraction would be less than 1 and the logarithm negative. A reduction is counted as a positive strain.

questions.prompt: The second pass takes the plate from 25 mm to 18 mm. What is its true strain, ln(25 / 18), to three decimal places?
hints: Divide 25 by 18 first.
Take the natural logarithm of 1.389.
ln(1.389) is a little under 0.33.
questions.onCorrect: The two true strains, 0.182 and 0.329, sum to 0.511, which is ln(30 / 18), the strain of rolling 30 mm to 18 mm in one pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is log base 10 of 1.389. True strain uses the natural logarithm.
That is the percent reduction as a fraction. True strain is a logarithm.

questions.prompt: A forging operation has a flow stress of 300 MPa on a contact area of 3000 mm2. Using force = flow stress x area, what is the force in kN?
hints: 1 MPa is 1 N per mm2, so the force comes out in newtons.
Multiply 300 by 3000.
Divide by 1000 to get kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 300 MPa x 3000 mm2 = 900,000 N, which is 900 kN.

questions.onCorrect: Forging forces are large: 900 kN is the weight of about 90 tonnes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in newtons. Divide by 1000 for kN.
That divides the area by the stress. The force is their product.

questions.prompt: A billet is forged at a flow stress of 250 MPa. Its area at the start is 2000 mm2, and the press squeezes it to half its height. Taking the flow stress as unchanged, what force is needed at the end, in kN?
hints: The volume is constant. What happens to the area when the height halves?
The area is now 4000 mm2.
Multiply by the flow stress and convert to kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Halving the height doubles the area to 4000 mm2, so the force is 250 x 4000 = 1,000,000 N = 1000 kN.

questions.onCorrect: The force doubles as the billet is squeezed, because the contact area doubles. Forging presses are rated for the force at the end of the stroke.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the starting area. The area has doubled by the end of the stroke.
That is the flow stress, in MPa. Multiply by the area for the force.

questions.prompt: Working a metal above its recrystallisation temperature, so that it softens as it deforms instead of hardening, is called what? Answer hot or cold.
hints: Cold working hardens a metal, as the wire drawing of an earlier lesson did.
questions.onCorrect: Above the recrystallisation temperature, which is roughly half the melting point in kelvin, new strain-free grains form as fast as dislocations pile up.

misconceptions.feedback: Cold working is done below the recrystallisation temperature, and it work hardens the metal. Softening as it deforms is the mark of the other kind.

questions.prompt: After a sheet is bent and the tool is removed, the bend opens slightly. What is this partial recovery called?
hints: Part of the strain was elastic, and the elastic part is recovered when the load is removed.
questions.onCorrect: To get a 90 degree bend, the sheet is bent a few degrees past 90 degrees, so that it springs back to the right angle.

misconceptions.feedback: Yielding is the permanent part of the deformation. The part that returns when the load is removed is elastic.

questions.prompt: A sheet 1.5 mm thick is bent through 90 degrees, which is pi / 2 radians, with an inner radius R = 2 mm and K = 0.4. The bend allowance is (pi / 2) x (R + K x t). What is it, in mm to two decimal places?
hints: Work out K x t = 0.4 x 1.5.
Add R to find the radius of the neutral axis.
Multiply by pi / 2, which is 1.571.
questions.onCorrect: The flat blank must include 4.08 mm of material for the bend, in addition to the lengths of the two flanges.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the inner radius of 2 mm and leaves out K x t. The neutral axis lies inside the sheet, at R + K x t.
That is the radius of the neutral axis. Multiply it by the angle in radians, pi / 2.

questions.prompt: A sheet 3 mm thick is bent through 60 degrees, which is pi / 3 radians, with R = 5 mm and K = 0.33. What is the bend allowance, in mm to two decimal places?
hints: Work out K x t = 0.33 x 3.
The angle in radians is pi / 3 = 1.047.
Multiply the radius of the neutral axis by the angle.
questions.onCorrect: A smaller angle gives a shorter arc, so a 60 degree bend takes less flat length than a 90 degree bend of the same radius.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 90 degrees. The angle here is 60 degrees, which is pi / 3 radians.
That is the radius of the neutral axis. Multiply it by the angle in radians.

questions.prompt: A plate is rolled from 40 mm to 25 mm thick. What is the true strain, ln(40 / 25), to three decimal places?
hints: Divide 40 by 25 first.
Take the natural logarithm of 1.6.
ln(1.6) is a little under 0.5.
questions.onCorrect: A true strain of 0.47 corresponds to a reduction of 37.5 percent, and the true strain is the quantity that adds from pass to pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is log base 10 of 1.6. True strain uses the natural logarithm.
That is the percent reduction as a fraction. True strain is a logarithm.

questions.prompt: A forging has a flow stress of 400 MPa and a contact area of 1500 mm2. What is the forging force, in kN?
hints: Multiply the flow stress by the area.
The product is in newtons.
Divide by 1000 for kN.
questions.onCorrect: The force scales directly with the flow stress, so a hot forging at a lower flow stress needs a smaller press.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in newtons. Divide by 1000 for kN.
That divides the area by the flow stress. The force is their product.

questions.prompt: A sheet 3 mm thick is bent through 90 degrees with an inner radius R = 4 mm and K = 0.40. What is the bend allowance, (pi / 2) x (R + K x t), in mm to two decimal places?
hints: Work out K x t = 0.40 x 3.
Add R to get the radius of the neutral axis.
Multiply by pi / 2.
questions.onCorrect: The neutral axis moves outward as K increases, so a larger K gives a longer bend allowance.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses R = 4 mm and leaves out K x t. The neutral axis lies at R + K x t.
That is the radius of the neutral axis. Multiply it by the angle in radians.

questions.prompt: A bar of diameter D = 30 mm is turned at N = 1200 rev/min. Using v = pi x D x N / 1000, what is the cutting speed, in m/min to one decimal place?
hints: The surface travels pi x D each revolution.
Multiply pi x 30 mm by 1200 revolutions each minute.
Divide by 1000 to convert mm to m.
questions.onCorrect: The cutting speed is the surface speed past the tool, and it sets how hot the cutting edge gets.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed in mm/min. Divide by 1000 for m/min.
That multiplies D by N and divides by 1000 without the factor of pi.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, the removal rate is 112,500 mm3/min. How many mm3 is that per second?
hints: There are 60 seconds in a minute.
Divide 112,500 by 60.
The answer is a little under 2000.
questions.onCorrect: Power in watts needs the removal rate in mm3 per second when the specific energy is in J/mm3.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 60. A per-second rate is smaller than a per-minute rate.

questions.prompt: A cut at 60 m/min with f = 0.1 mm/rev and d = 1 mm removes 6000 mm3/min, which is 100 mm3/s. With a specific cutting energy of 2.5 J/mm3, what power is needed, in W?
hints: Power is specific energy times removal rate.
The units are J/mm3 times mm3/s, which is J/s.
Multiply 2.5 by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Small cuts need little power, so a light machine can take them, but the same energy goes into a smaller chip.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the removal rate per minute. For watts, use mm3 per second.
That multiplies by 6000 mm3/min and divides by 25 s. Use the rate in mm3 per second.

questions.prompt: A cutting speed is raised by 20 percent. What is the likely change in tool life, for a typical tool tipped with hard tungsten carbide?
hints: Taylor's equation raises the speed to a power of -1 / n.
With n about 0.25, that power is -4.
questions.onCorrect: Taylor's rule gives 1.2 to the power -4, which is 0.48, so the tool lasts about half as long.

misconceptions.feedback: Tool life falls much faster than speed rises, because the wear grows steeply with the temperature at the edge.
Hardness does not protect the edge. The wear rate rises sharply with cutting speed.

choices.label: It falls by about half.
It does not change, because the tool is hard.
It falls by about 17 percent, in proportion to the speed.

questions.prompt: For a tool with Taylor exponent n = 0.25, the life changes by a factor of (speed ratio) to the power -1 / n = -4. The cutting speed rises 10 percent, so the speed ratio is 1.1. What is the factor in tool life, to two decimal places?
hints: The speed ratio is 1.1, and the exponent is -4.
Take the reciprocal.
questions.onCorrect: A 10 percent rise in speed costs about a third of the tool life.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 1.1 to the power +4. Tool life falls with speed, so the exponent is negative.
That is 1 / 1.1. The exponent is -4, not -1.

questions.prompt: Run the tool the other way. With n = 0.25, the cutting speed is cut by 20 percent, so the speed ratio is 0.8. What is the factor in tool life, to two decimal places?
hints: The speed ratio is 0.8 and the exponent is -4.
Take the reciprocal.
questions.onCorrect: Slowing the cut by a fifth more than doubles the tool life, though the part takes a quarter longer to cut.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 1 / 0.8. The exponent is -4, not -1.
That is 0.8 to the power +4. A slower speed lengthens tool life.

questions.prompt: The theoretical roughness of a turned surface is Ra = f^2 / (32 r), with f the feed and r the tool nose radius, both in mm. For f = 0.2 mm/rev and r = 0.8 mm, what is Ra in micrometres, to two decimal places?
hints: Square the feed: 0.2 x 0.2.
Divide by 32 x 0.8 = 25.6.
The result is in mm. Multiply by 1000 for micrometres.
questions.onCorrect: The roughness depends on the feed and the nose radius, and not on the cutting speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Ra in millimetres. Multiply by 1000 for micrometres.
That divides by r alone, leaving out the factor of 32.

questions.prompt: The theoretical roughness of a turned surface is Ra = f^2 / (32 r). The feed is halved from 0.2 to 0.1 mm/rev, with the same nose radius r = 0.8 mm. What is Ra now, in micrometres to two decimal places?
hints: Square the new feed: 0.1 x 0.1.
Divide by 25.6.
Convert mm to micrometres.
questions.onCorrect: Halving the feed cuts Ra to one quarter, because the feed is squared, but it doubles the time the cut takes.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves Ra. The feed is squared, so halving it quarters Ra.
That is the roughness at f = 0.2 mm. Halving the feed changes it.

questions.prompt: A bar of diameter D = 80 mm is turned at N = 400 rev/min. What is the cutting speed, in m/min to one decimal place?
hints: Multiply pi x 80 mm by 400 revolutions.
The result is in mm/min.
Divide by 1000.
questions.onCorrect: At this speed a carbide tool will cut steel at a typical rate, but its life depends strongly on the exact value.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed in mm/min. Divide by 1000 for m/min.
That multiplies D by N without the factor of pi and without converting to m.

questions.prompt: A cut is made at v = 120 m/min, f = 0.25 mm/rev and d = 1.5 mm, in a material with a specific cutting energy of 4 J/mm3. The removal rate is v x f x d, with v in mm/min. What power is needed, in kW to one decimal place?
hints: Convert 120 m/min to mm/min.
Multiply by f and d, then divide by 60 for mm3/s.
Multiply by 4 J/mm3, then divide by 1000 for kW.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: v = 120,000 mm/min, so the removal rate is 120,000 x 0.25 x 1.5 = 45,000 mm3/min = 750 mm3/s. Power = 4 x 750 = 3000 W = 3.0 kW.

questions.onCorrect: At 3 kW the cut needs a machine with a spindle motor well above that, since the machine itself loses some power.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the removal rate per minute with the energy. Power needs the rate per second.
That is the removal rate in cm3 per second. Multiply by 4 J/mm3 and convert units.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the feed in turning?
hints: Feed is measured in mm per revolution.

acceptedIdeas: The distance the tool advances in each revolution of the work.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The distance the tool advances in each revolution of the work.

questions.onCorrect: Feed, speed and depth are the three settings of a cut, and the removal rate is their product.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cutting speed, in m/min.
That is the depth of cut.
That is the spindle speed, in rev/min.

choices.label: The distance the tool advances in each revolution of the work.
The number of times the work turns in a minute.
The speed of the surface of the work past the tool.
The depth to which the tool cuts into the work.

questions.prompt: An injection moulded part has a projected area of 80 cm2, which is 8000 mm2, and the cavity pressure is 40 MPa. What clamp force is needed, in kN?
hints: 1 MPa is 1 N per mm2, so the force comes out in newtons.
Multiply 40 by 8000.
Divide by 1000 to get kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Force = pressure x area = 40 MPa x 8000 mm2 = 320,000 N = 320 kN.

questions.onCorrect: The clamp has to resist the pressure over the whole projected area, which is why large flat parts need big machines.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in newtons. Divide by 1000 for kN.
That divides the pressure by the area. The force is their product.

questions.prompt: Tooling for a mould costs 20,000 dollars. A moulded part then costs 1.50 each, and a printed part costs 12 each with no tooling. For 1000 parts, which route has the lower total cost?
hints: Add the tooling to the moulded total before comparing.
Moulded total: 20,000 + 1.50 x 1000. Printed total: 12 x 1000.
questions.onCorrect: At 1000 parts the tooling has not yet paid back, and printing is cheaper by 9,500 dollars.

misconceptions.feedback: The moulded total is 20,000 + 1.50 x 1000 = 21,500 dollars, because the tooling has to be paid for as well.
Only printing has a flat cost per part. Moulding has a large cost paid at the start.

choices.label: Moulding, because the cost per part is lower.
Printing, at 12,000 dollars in total.
They cost the same, because the cost per part is flat.

questions.prompt: In the worked example the printed part costs 9.90 and the moulded part 2.40. How much does each moulded part save, in dollars?
hints: Subtract the moulded cost from the printed cost.
The saving is the difference, not the sum.
9.90 - 2.40 is a little over 7.
questions.onCorrect: The tooling is paid back at this rate: each part made by moulding saves 7.50 dollars.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two costs. The saving is the difference.

questions.prompt: Tooling costs 45,000 dollars. A moulded part costs 0.80 and a printed part costs 5.80. The saving per part is 5.00 dollars. At how many parts does moulding break even?
hints: Break-even is the tooling cost divided by the saving per part.
Divide 45,000 by 5.
The answer is a whole number of thousands.
questions.onCorrect: Past 9000 parts every extra part moulded rather than printed saves 5.00 dollars.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 5.80, the printed cost. Divide by the saving per part, 5.00.
That divides by 0.80, the moulded cost. Divide by the saving per part.

questions.prompt: In the first example the mould cost 20,000 dollars, moulded parts cost 1.50 and printed parts 12, and break-even is 1905 parts. The mould turns out to cost 40,000 dollars, with the part costs unchanged. What is the new break-even volume, in parts to the nearest whole part?
hints: The saving per part is still 10.50 dollars.
Divide the new tooling cost by the saving.
Doubling the tooling doubles the break-even.
questions.onCorrect: Break-even is proportional to the tooling cost, so a mould that costs twice as much needs twice the volume.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the earlier break-even, for the cheaper mould. The tooling cost has doubled.
That divides by 12, the printed cost. Divide by the saving per part, 10.50.

questions.prompt: The slight taper on the walls of a moulded part, so that it releases from the mould, is called what?
hints: Without it the walls rub on the mould as the part comes out.
questions.onCorrect: A draft of 0.5 to 2 degrees is usual, and the rougher the surface of the mould, the more draft is needed.

misconceptions.feedback: A fillet rounds a corner. The taper on the walls, along the direction in which the mould opens, has a different name.

questions.prompt: A mould wall 25 mm tall has a draft of 2 degrees. The face moves by height x tan(draft). How far, in mm to two decimal places?
hints: The tangent of 2 degrees is about 0.0349.
Multiply by 25.
The shift is under a millimetre.
questions.onCorrect: A 1 degree draft on a 40 mm wall moves the face by 0.70 mm, and 2 degrees on 25 mm by 0.87 mm, which adds up over a part.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shift for twice the angle. Use tan(2 degrees), which is 0.0349.
That multiplies by the angle in degrees. Use the tangent of the angle.

questions.prompt: A part has a projected area of 150 cm2, which is 15,000 mm2, and the cavity pressure is 35 MPa. What clamp force is needed, in kN?
hints: Multiply the pressure by the area in mm2.
The product is in newtons.
Divide by 1000 for kN.
questions.onCorrect: Machines are rated by their clamp force, and this part would need one of at least 525 kN, plus a margin.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in newtons. Divide by 1000 for kN.
That divides the pressure by the area. The force is their product.

questions.prompt: Tooling costs 30,000 dollars. A moulded part costs 2.00 and a printed part costs 12.00. At how many parts does moulding break even?
hints: The saving per part is 12 - 2.
Divide the tooling cost by the saving.
The answer is a whole number of thousands.
questions.onCorrect: Above 3000 parts moulding is cheaper in total, and below it printing is.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 14, the sum of the two costs. Divide by the saving, 10.
That divides by 12, the printed cost. Divide by the saving per part.

questions.prompt: A complex part is needed in a run of 200. A mould would cost 30,000 dollars, and the part costs 12 to print. Which process fits best?
hints: Compare 200 parts with the break-even volume of 3000 for these costs.

acceptedIdeas: 3D printing, because no tooling is needed.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 3D printing, because no tooling is needed.

questions.onCorrect: Moulding has a high cost paid up front and wins only above the break-even volume.

misconceptions.feedback: The lowest cost per part is reached only when the tooling is spread over many parts. At 200 parts the tooling dominates.
A long mould life does not help when only 200 parts are wanted, since the tooling is paid for in full.
No process is always the cheapest, and it depends on the volume and the shape.

choices.label: Machining from solid, because it is always the cheapest.
Injection moulding, because moulds last for years.
Injection moulding, because it has the lowest cost per part.
3D printing, because no tooling is needed.

questions.prompt: A process has a mean of 25.00 mm and a standard deviation of 0.015 mm. The upper limit is 25.06 mm. How many standard deviations is the upper limit from the mean?
hints: Find the distance from the mean to the limit.
Divide that distance by the standard deviation.
The distance is 0.06 mm.
questions.onCorrect: A normal distribution has only about 3 parts in 100,000 beyond 4 standard deviations on one side.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance in mm. Divide it by the standard deviation of 0.015 mm to count the sigmas.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, sigma is 0.03 mm. What is 6 x sigma, in mm?
hints: Multiply the standard deviation by 6.
6 x 0.03 is under two tenths of a millimetre.
Write it in mm.
questions.onCorrect: This is the width of the range that holds 99.73 percent of the parts, which is compared with the tolerance range.

misconceptions.feedback: That is sigma itself. Multiply it by 6.

questions.prompt: A process has a standard deviation of 0.01 mm and a tolerance of plus or minus 0.03 mm, so USL - LSL = 0.06 mm. What is Cp, to two decimal places?
hints: Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 sigma).
6 sigma = 0.06 mm.
Divide 0.06 by 0.06.
questions.onCorrect: A Cp of 1.0 means the 6 sigma spread of the process exactly fills the tolerance, so it has no margin.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the tolerance range by 12 sigma. Cp uses 6 sigma.
That divides by sigma alone. Cp divides the tolerance range by 6 sigma.

questions.prompt: A process has a standard deviation of 0.01 mm and limits of 24.95 and 25.05 mm, so its Cp is 1.67, but its mean has drifted to 25.04 mm. What do you expect?
hints: How many standard deviations are there between the mean and the upper limit?
About 16 percent of a normal distribution lies more than 1 standard deviation above the mean.

acceptedIdeas: About one part in six is above the upper limit.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About one part in six is above the upper limit.

questions.onCorrect: Cp compares the spread with the tolerance range and ignores centring, so a capable process can still make bad parts.

misconceptions.feedback: Cp ignores where the mean sits. With the mean at 25.04 the upper limit is only 1 standard deviation away.
Half of the parts would be above the mean, 25.04, but the limit is 25.05, which is above that.

choices.label: About half of the parts are outside the limits.
Almost every part is within the limits, because Cp is well above 1.
About one part in six is above the upper limit.

questions.prompt: A process has mean 24.985 mm, standard deviation 0.01 mm and limits 24.95 and 25.05 mm. The nearer limit is 0.035 mm away, and Cpk = (distance to the nearer limit) / (3 sigma). What is Cpk, to two decimal places?
hints: The lower limit is the nearer one: 24.985 - 24.95.
3 sigma = 0.03 mm.
Divide the distance by 3 sigma.
questions.onCorrect: This process has drifted low, so the lower limit is the nearer one, and Cpk is about 1.17 against a Cp of 1.67.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the farther limit, the upper one at 0.065 mm. Cpk uses the nearer limit.
That divides by 9 sigma. Cpk divides by 3 sigma.

questions.prompt: A different process has a standard deviation of 0.008 mm and limits 24.95 and 25.05 mm. It had drifted off centre and is now recentred, so that its mean is 25.00 mm. What is Cpk now, to two decimal places?
hints: Both limits are the same distance from a centred mean.
The distance is 0.05 mm.
Divide by 3 sigma = 0.024 mm.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both limits are 0.05 mm away, so Cpk = 0.05 / 0.024 = 2.08, which equals Cp.

questions.onCorrect: When a process is centred, Cpk equals Cp, and any shift of the mean lowers Cpk below Cp.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value for the lesson's process, with sigma 0.01 mm. This process has sigma 0.008 mm, so 3 sigma is 0.024 mm.
That divides by 1.5 sigma. Cpk divides by 3 sigma.

questions.prompt: Which capability index accounts for how far the process mean sits from the nearer limit, and so falls when the process drifts off centre?
hints: It is Cp with a k added for the centring.
questions.onCorrect: Cpk is never larger than Cp, and the two are equal only when the mean sits exactly at the middle of the tolerance.

misconceptions.feedback: Cp compares only the spread with the tolerance range and ignores where the mean is.

questions.prompt: A part has a tolerance of 10.00 plus or minus 0.04 mm, and the process has a standard deviation of 0.01 mm. What is Cp, to two decimal places?
hints: USL - LSL = 0.08 mm.
6 sigma = 0.06 mm.
Divide 0.08 by 0.06.
questions.onCorrect: A Cp of 1.33 means the 8 sigma tolerance range holds a 6 sigma process with some margin, a common target.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 12 sigma. Cp divides the tolerance range by 6 sigma.
That divides by 3 sigma. Cp divides the tolerance range by 6 sigma.

questions.prompt: The same process, with limits 9.96 and 10.04 mm and sigma 0.01 mm, runs with its mean at 10.02 mm. What is Cpk, to two decimal places?
hints: Find which limit is nearer: 10.04 - 10.02 or 10.02 - 9.96.
The nearer distance is 0.02 mm.
Divide by 3 sigma = 0.03 mm.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The upper limit is the nearer, 0.02 mm away: Cpk = 0.02 / (3 x 0.01) = 0.67.

questions.onCorrect: A Cpk below 1 means the nearer limit is under 3 standard deviations from the mean, and many parts will be out of limits.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the farther limit, the lower one at 0.06 mm. Cpk uses the nearer limit.
That is the Cp, which ignores the shift of the mean.

questions.prompt: A process has Cp = 1.5 and Cpk = 0.5. What does this say about it?
hints: Compare Cp, which ignores centring, with Cpk, which does not.

acceptedIdeas: Its spread is small enough, but its mean is off centre.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its spread is small enough, but its mean is off centre.

questions.onCorrect: Recentring the mean would bring Cpk up towards the Cp of 1.5, without any change to the spread.

misconceptions.feedback: A Cp of 1.5 means the spread fits well within the tolerance range. The low Cpk comes from the position of the mean.
Cpk of 0.5 means the nearer limit is only 1.5 standard deviations from the mean, so a good many parts fall outside.
Measuring more parts only gives a better estimate of Cpk. The process has to be centred to change it.

choices.label: Measuring more parts will raise the Cpk.
Its spread is too wide for the tolerance.
It is making no parts out of limits.
Its spread is small enough, but its mean is off centre.

questions.prompt: A designer wants the lightest beam for a given stiffness. The performance index is sqrt(E) / density, with E in GPa and density in g/cm3. For steel, E = 210 GPa and density 7.85 g/cm3. What is the index, to two decimal places?
hints: Take the square root of 210.
Divide by the density, 7.85.
The square root of 210 is a little over 14.
questions.onCorrect: Steel has the lowest index of the common materials in the next screens, which is why it makes heavy stiff beams.

misconceptions.feedback: That is E divided by density, the index for a tie rod in tension. The beam index uses the square root of E.
That is the square root of E alone. Divide it by the density.

questions.prompt: A beam of aluminium is made as stiff as a steel beam of the same length and a similar shape. Aluminium is about a third as dense as steel and about a third as stiff. Roughly how does the mass of the aluminium beam compare with the steel one?
hints: A less stiff material needs a larger section to bend as little.
Ask whether the section has to grow as much as the density falls.

acceptedIdeas: It is lighter, but well over a third of the mass.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is lighter, but well over a third of the mass.

questions.onCorrect: The aluminium beam has about 0.60 of the steel beam's mass, a saving of 40 percent where density alone would suggest 66 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: The section is larger, about 1.73 times the area, but each cubic centimetre weighs only about a third as much, so the beam still comes out lighter.
A third of the mass would follow if the two beams were the same size, but the aluminium beam needs a larger section to be as stiff, so it weighs more than a third of the steel one.
A beam's stiffness grows with the fourth power of its side, so a modest increase in section makes up for the lower stiffness and the mass grows by less than the density falls.

choices.label: It is about a third of the mass, in proportion to the density.
It is lighter, but well over a third of the mass.
It is heavier, because it needs a larger section.
It is about the same, because the lower density and the lower stiffness cancel out.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, E = 70 GPa for aluminium. What is the square root of 70, to two decimal places?
hints: 8 x 8 = 64 and 9 x 9 = 81, so the root is between 8 and 9.
It is a little more than 8.3.
Round to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: The square root is divided by the density in the next step.

misconceptions.feedback: That is half of 70. The square root is smaller than that.

questions.prompt: Magnesium has E = 45 GPa and density 1.74 g/cm3. What is sqrt(E) / density, to two decimal places?
hints: The square root of 45 is 6.708.
Divide by 1.74.
The answer is between 3 and 4.
questions.onCorrect: At 3.86 magnesium beats aluminium by about a quarter, though it stays far behind the carbon-fibre composite and the wood.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides E by density without taking the square root of E.
That is the square root of E alone. Divide it by the density.

questions.prompt: A tie rod carrying a tension load is chosen for stiffness at minimum mass, and its index is E / density. Compare an aluminium rod (E = 70, density 2.70) with a steel rod (E = 210, density 7.85) of equal stiffness and length. What is the aluminium rod's mass as a multiple of the steel rod's, to two decimal places?
hints: For a rod in tension the mass varies as density / E.
Work out density / E for each metal.
Divide the aluminium value by the steel value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mass varies as density / E, so the ratio is (2.70 / 70) / (7.85 / 210) = 0.03857 / 0.03738 = 1.03.

questions.onCorrect: For a tie rod, aluminium offers no saving, because the index E / density is nearly the same for the two metals.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio for a beam in bending, which uses the square root of E. A rod in tension uses E itself.
That is the ratio of the densities alone. The rod must also be larger to match the stiffness.

questions.prompt: A single complex metal prototype is wanted, with no tooling to pay for. Which process fits best?
hints: With only one part, any tooling cost falls entirely on that part.
questions.onCorrect: Additive manufacturing has no tooling, so cost per part is flat, and it can make shapes that no mould could release.

misconceptions.feedback: A die costs tens of thousands of dollars, which for a single part is far more than printing.
Closed-die forging needs a pair of dies shaped for the part, so for one prototype their cost would outweigh everything else.

choices.label: Metal 3D printing
Die casting
Forging in closed dies

questions.prompt: A glass-fibre composite has E = 40 GPa and density 1.9 g/cm3. What is sqrt(E) / density, to two decimal places?
hints: Take the square root of 40.
Divide by the density, 1.9.
The root is a little over 6.
questions.onCorrect: The glass-fibre composite ranks just above aluminium on this index and far below carbon fibre, because glass fibres are much less stiff than carbon ones.

misconceptions.feedback: That is E divided by density, the index for a tie rod in tension. The beam index uses the square root of E.
That is the square root of E alone. Divide it by the density.

questions.prompt: Using the index sqrt(E) / density, which of steel (1.85), aluminium (3.10), carbon-fibre composite (6.45) and pine (6.32) gives the lightest beam for a given stiffness?
hints: The best material has the highest index.
questions.onCorrect: Pine is a close second, and in practice cost, corrosion and the process may decide between the two.

misconceptions.feedback: Steel has the highest E of the four, but also the highest density, and its index is the lowest.
Aluminium beats steel but not the composite or the pine, once the larger section needed for stiffness is allowed for.
Pine is very close at 6.32, but the composite's index of 6.45 is slightly higher.

choices.label: Aluminium, because it has the lowest density of the metals.
Pine, because wood is the lightest.
Carbon-fibre composite
Steel, because it has the highest stiffness.

questions.prompt: About 100,000 thin-walled aluminium housings with a complex shape are needed every year. Which process fits?
hints: At this volume the tooling cost is shared among a great many parts.
questions.onCorrect: Die casting pays for a steel die once and then makes each housing cheaply, which suits aluminium at high volume.

misconceptions.feedback: Printing has a flat cost per part that is far higher than a cast part at this volume.
Machining each housing would waste most of the material and take a long time per part.
Sand casting has a rougher surface and looser tolerance, and it needs a new mould for each part.

choices.label: Die casting
Sand casting
3D printing
Machining from solid

flashcards.front: What is the highest engineering stress on a stress-strain curve called?
flashcards.back: It is the ultimate tensile strength, reached when necking begins.

flashcards.front: A 25 mm gauge length measures 30 mm at fracture. What is the percent elongation?
flashcards.back: (30 - 25) / 25 = 0.20, so the elongation is 20 percent.

flashcards.front: Why does toughness differ from strength?
flashcards.back: Strength is a stress, while toughness is the area under the curve, the energy absorbed per volume before fracture.

flashcards.front: Which kind of bond lets layers of atoms slide in a metal?
flashcards.back: Metallic bonding is not tied to a pair of atoms, so layers can slide and the metal deforms.

flashcards.front: Specific stiffness of a material with E = 60 GPa and density 2.4 g/cm3?
Why can strong bonds go with a brittle material?
flashcards.back: Strong bonds give a high stiffness, but if they resist sliding the material cannot deform plastically, so a crack grows instead.

flashcards.front: What is the defect whose movement lets a metal deform plastically?
flashcards.back: A dislocation moves a row at a time, so far less stress is needed than for sliding a whole plane.

flashcards.front: Strength = 50 + 20 / square root of d. d = 0.01 mm. Strength in MPa?
Why does work hardening raise strength but lower ductility?
flashcards.back: Cold work multiplies dislocations that tangle and block each other, which makes slip harder and leaves less capacity to deform further.

flashcards.front: Which structure forms when steel is quenched?
flashcards.back: Fast cooling traps carbon in the iron lattice as martensite, which is very hard and brittle.

flashcards.front: A 0.40 percent carbon steel cooled slowly: fraction of pearlite, to three decimal places?
Why does tempering follow quenching?
flashcards.back: Quenched martensite is hard but brittle, and reheating lets some carbon leave it, which gives up a little hardness for much more toughness.

flashcards.front: What is the temperature called, below which a polymer is stiff and glassy?
flashcards.back: Below the glass transition temperature the chains cannot move, so the polymer is hard and stiff.

flashcards.front: Stiffness along the fibres: Ef = 100 GPa, Em = 4 GPa, 50 percent fibre?
Why is a composite so much stiffer along its fibres than across them?
flashcards.back: Along the fibres the stiff fibres share the strain and carry most of the load, but across them the load passes through the soft matrix in series.

flashcards.front: What property of a material gives the stress intensity at which a crack runs?
flashcards.back: Fracture toughness K_IC, in MPa times the square root of metres, is the stress intensity at which a crack grows.

flashcards.front: K_IC = 50 MPa sqrt(m), a = 2 mm, Y = 1. Critical stress in MPa to the nearest 10?
flashcards.back: 50 / sqrt(pi x 0.002) = 631, which is 630 to the nearest 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 / sqrt(pi x 0.002) = 631, which is 630 to the nearest 10.

flashcards.front: Why can a small crack be dangerous in a strong material?
flashcards.back: Stress piles up at the crack tip, and a strong material with low toughness can have a critical stress at the tip far below its yield strength.

flashcards.front: In a corrosion cell, which electrode loses metal?
flashcards.back: The anode is the electrode where the metal dissolves as ions and releases electrons.

flashcards.front: Iron (M = 55.85, n = 2) loses 0.01 A for 1000 s. Grams lost, to three decimal places?
Why does a scratched coating of zinc still protect steel but a scratched coating of paint may not?
flashcards.back: Zinc is the more active metal, so it is the anode and corrodes in the steel's place, but paint is only a barrier and the exposed steel rusts beneath it.

flashcards.front: A casting section is made three times thicker, so V / A triples. By what factor does the freezing time change?
flashcards.back: Time goes as (V / A)^2, so it changes by 3 squared, which is 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Time goes as (V / A)^2, so it changes by 3 squared, which is 9.

flashcards.front: A pattern is 200 mm and the metal shrinks 1 percent. How long is the casting?
Why must the riser freeze after the casting?
flashcards.back: The riser must stay liquid long enough to feed the casting as it shrinks, so the shrinkage hole ends up in the riser.

flashcards.front: Rolling from 12 mm to 8 mm: true strain to three decimal places?
What is it called when a bent sheet opens slightly after the tool is removed?
flashcards.back: Springback is the recovery of the elastic part of the strain, so sheets are bent slightly past the target angle.

flashcards.front: Why does forging need more force as it proceeds?
flashcards.back: The volume is constant, so as the billet gets shorter its contact area grows, and force is flow stress times area.

flashcards.front: Material removal rate: v = 100 m/min, f = 0.2 mm/rev, d = 1 mm. In cm3/min?
Taylor, n = 0.25: speed ratio 0.9. Factor in tool life, two decimals?
Why is faster cutting not always cheaper per part?
flashcards.back: Tool life falls much faster than speed rises, so the cost of worn tools and tool changes can outweigh the time saved.

flashcards.front: Clamp force for 200 cm2 (20,000 mm2) at 25 MPa, in kN?
Break-even: tooling 10,000, moulded 1.00, printed 6.00. How many parts?
Why does the cost per part fall as the run gets longer when moulding?
flashcards.back: The tooling cost is fixed, so it is shared among more parts, while the moulded cost per part stays the same.

flashcards.front: Which index compares the width of the tolerance range with 6 sigma?
flashcards.back: Cp is (USL - LSL) divided by 6 sigma, and it ignores where the mean sits.

flashcards.front: A process has a standard deviation of 0.02 mm and a tolerance range of 0.12 mm. Cp?
Why can a process with Cp above 1 still make parts out of tolerance?
flashcards.back: Cp ignores the mean, so a process that is off centre can have a nearer limit that is only a little way from the mean and so make many bad parts.

flashcards.front: Index sqrt(E) / density for a material with E = 64 GPa and density 2.0 g/cm3?
Which kind of process suits a few thousand or more parts of a plastic, once its tooling has been paid for?
flashcards.back: Injection moulding has high tooling cost and low cost per part, so it suits large volumes.

flashcards.front: Why should material and process be chosen together?
flashcards.back: The process limits which materials and shapes are possible, and the material limits which processes can be used, so each choice changes the other.
